name: Two-Stage Rocket
overview:
A rocket is a machine for carrying something into orbit by throwing mass out of its back very fast. Its engines burn fuel and liquid oxygen and blast the hot gas out through bell-shaped nozzles; pushing that gas backwards pushes the rocket forwards. Reaching orbit means hitting about 28,000 km/h sideways, so most of a rocket is propellant tanks.

This one has two stages. The first stage, with nine engines, lifts everything off the pad and through the thick lower atmosphere, then separates about two and a half minutes in. It flips around, relights its engines, unfolds its grid fins to steer, and lands on four legs so it can fly again. The second stage, with a single engine built for vacuum, finishes the climb to orbit.

The satellite rides on top inside the payload fairing, a nose cone in two halves that shields it from air friction and buffeting. Once the rocket is above most of the atmosphere the fairing splits open and falls away, and the satellite is later released on its own.

parts.description: One of two carbon-composite clamshell halves that shield the satellite through the atmosphere, then split apart and fall away.

details.didYouKnow: A recovered fairing half is worth several million dollars, which is why some launch companies chase them across the ocean with boats.
details.howItWorks: Together the two halves form the rocket's nose cone, taking the air pressure, heating and buffeting so the delicate satellite never feels the wind. Once the rocket is above almost all of the atmosphere, latches along the seam and at the base let go and the halves swing apart and fall away. On rockets like this each half can carry small thrusters and a steerable parachute so it can be fished out of the sea and flown again.
keyNumbers: About 13 m tall and 5 m wide when closed
Jettisoned roughly 3 to 4 minutes after launch
Each half weighs roughly 1 tonne
details.madeOf: A sandwich of thin carbon-fibre skins over an aluminium honeycomb core, which is extremely stiff for its weight. Every kilogram of fairing that rides to space is a kilogram less satellite, so lightness matters.

parts.name: Fairing half

parts.description: Pneumatic pusher rail running up the seam; it drives the two halves apart at jettison.

details.didYouKnow: Older fairings were split with explosive cords; pneumatic systems were adopted partly because they make far less shock and dust near a clean satellite.
details.howItWorks: When the flight computer commands jettison, the latches holding the halves together release and gas-driven pushers along this rail shove the halves apart. Using pressurised gas rather than explosives gives a gentle, clean push that does not shake the satellite or scatter debris onto it. The rail also stiffens the seam so the two halves stay sealed and aligned during the buffeting of ascent.
keyNumbers: Runs roughly 10 m up the fairing seam
Opens the fairing in well under a second
Works at altitudes above about 100 km
details.madeOf: Steel and aluminium fittings with pneumatic pistons, fed from a small high-pressure gas bottle. Steel is used where the push loads concentrate.

parts.name: Separation rail

parts.description: The spacecraft's body: structure, batteries, propellant and electronics wrapped in gold multi-layer insulation.

details.didYouKnow: The gold colour usually is not gold at all: it is plastic film coated with aluminium on one side, with an amber tint from the plastic itself.
details.howItWorks: The bus is the satellite's chassis and life-support system: it holds the batteries, propellant tanks, flight computer, radios and attitude-control gear that keep the mission alive. Everything else, like the antenna and solar arrays, bolts onto it. During launch its base sits on the payload adapter, so all its weight and the rocket's shaking pass through that ring.
keyNumbers: A large communications satellite weighs about 3 to 6 tonnes
Often carries more than half its launch mass as propellant
Designed to work for about 15 years
details.madeOf: A frame of aluminium honeycomb panels and carbon-fibre tubes, wrapped in multi-layer insulation of thin gold- or silver-coloured plastic films. The blanket reflects sunlight and holds in warmth so the electronics stay at a comfortable temperature.

parts.name: Satellite bus

parts.description: Stowed solar wing; after release it unfolds to power the satellite.

details.didYouKnow: Solar panels lose a little power every year because radiation in space slowly damages the cells, so they are sized for the end of the mission, not the start.
details.howItWorks: During launch each wing is folded flat against the side of the bus like a closed concertina and pinned down by hold-down bolts. After separation the bolts are released and springs or motors swing the panels out, then a drive motor keeps them turned towards the Sun as the satellite orbits. The power they make charges the batteries and runs everything aboard.
keyNumbers: Wings can span about 30 m or more once open
Can generate roughly 10 to 20 kilowatts in total
Space-grade cells convert about 30 percent of sunlight
details.madeOf: High-efficiency multi-junction gallium arsenide solar cells bonded to lightweight carbon-fibre honeycomb panels. These cells stack several layers that each harvest a different colour of light.

parts.name: Folded solar array

parts.description: Parabolic reflector that beams data to ground stations.

details.didYouKnow: Large dishes that will not fit in the fairing are folded during launch and spring open in orbit, a bit like an umbrella.
details.howItWorks: The dish is a curved mirror for radio waves: signals from the feed horn bounce off its shaped surface and leave as a tight beam aimed at a region of Earth. Incoming signals are focused back onto the feed in the same way. Because it is so directional, the satellite's pointing system must keep it aimed very precisely.
keyNumbers: Typically about 2 to 3 m across
Surface shape accurate to under a millimetre
Faces temperature swings of over 200 °C
details.madeOf: Usually a carbon-fibre reflector, because it barely changes shape as it swings between blazing sun and deep cold. The surface may be coated to reflect radio waves while staying thermally stable.

parts.name: High-gain antenna dish

parts.description: Feed that illuminates the dish; sits at its focal point.

details.didYouKnow: The ridged inner walls of many horns are there to shape the beam evenly, so less energy spills past the edge of the dish.
details.howItWorks: The feed horn is where radio signals actually enter and leave the satellite's electronics. It sits at the dish's focal point and sprays its signal across the reflector, which then bounces it out as a narrow beam. On the way back, the dish collects faint signals from the ground and concentrates them into the horn.
keyNumbers: Works at frequencies of roughly 10 to 30 gigahertz
Opening only a few centimetres to tens of centimetres wide
Handles transmitter power of typically tens to hundreds of watts
details.madeOf: Precision-machined aluminium or titanium, sometimes plated, because the inside shape must match the radio wavelength closely and stay that way through big temperature swings.

parts.name: Antenna feed horn

parts.description: Camera that photographs star fields to work out which way the satellite points.

details.didYouKnow: Sailors navigated by the stars for centuries; star trackers do the same job automatically, comparing what they see with a catalogue of thousands of stars.
details.howItWorks: Each tracker is a small digital camera that snaps the sky, picks out bright stars and matches their pattern against an onboard star catalogue. From that match it works out the satellite's exact orientation many times a second. Two are fitted so that if one is blinded by the Sun or Moon, the other can still see.
keyNumbers: Accurate to a few arcseconds, a tiny fraction of a degree
Updates its fix about 10 times a second
Typically weighs about 1 to 3 kg
details.madeOf: A sensitive image sensor and lens inside a metal housing, topped with a long baffle tube painted matt black to block stray sunlight.

parts.name: Star tracker

parts.description: Small rocket engine the satellite fires to climb into its final orbit.

details.didYouKnow: Some newer satellites skip this engine and spiral up slowly using electric thrusters instead, which can take several months but save a lot of propellant.
details.howItWorks: The rocket usually leaves a communications satellite in a stretched transfer orbit, and this engine does the rest. Fired several times at the high point of the orbit, it raises the low point until the orbit is circular, often at geostationary height. It burns two propellants that ignite on contact, so there is no spark plug to fail.
keyNumbers: Typically about 400 to 500 newtons of thrust
Can fire for a total of over an hour across several burns
Raises the orbit to about 36,000 km on geostationary missions
details.madeOf: A titanium or high-temperature alloy body with a nozzle of heat-resistant metal such as a niobium or platinum alloy, which can glow hot without melting.

parts.name: Apogee thruster

parts.description: Cone that carries the satellite's loads into the stage and holds the separation system.

details.didYouKnow: Adapters come in standard sizes so the same satellite design can launch on rockets from different companies.
details.howItWorks: The adapter narrows from the stage's width down to the ring the satellite sits on, funnelling every bump and vibration of launch into the stage structure. It carries the clamp band, separation springs and the electrical connectors that keep the satellite charged and monitored until release. After separation it stays behind on the upper stage.
keyNumbers: Satellite interface ring roughly 1.6 m across
Carries loads of up to about 6 g on ascent
Typically weighs around 100 kg or less
details.madeOf: Aluminium or carbon-fibre composite, often with honeycomb stiffening. It must be stiff enough to stop the satellite wobbling at frequencies that could damage it.

parts.name: Payload adapter

parts.description: Tensioned ring that grips the satellite until pyrotechnic bolts release it.

details.didYouKnow: The sudden release of the band can cause the sharpest jolt the satellite feels in the whole launch, so engineers work hard to make it gentle.
details.howItWorks: The band wraps around matching lips on the adapter and the satellite and is pulled tight like a giant hose clamp, locking them together. At release, small pyrotechnic bolt-cutters snap the tensioning bolts, the band springs open, and compressed springs in the adapter push the satellite gently away. Catcher springs hold the loose band so it does not float off as debris.
keyNumbers: Tensioned to roughly 20 to 40 kilonewtons
Pushes the satellite off at under 1 m/s
Releases in a few milliseconds
details.madeOf: Steel or titanium straps with aluminium clamp shoes, because the band must hold enormous tension without stretching.

parts.name: Clamp band

parts.description: Top ring of the upper stage; mounts the avionics and the fairing.

details.didYouKnow: Putting the computers up here keeps them far from the hot, vibrating engine bay at the other end of the stage.
details.howItWorks: The forward skirt is a short cylinder above the fuel tank that turns the top of the stage into a mounting deck. The fairing's base bolts to its outer edge and the payload adapter sits on top, so it carries the satellite's weight and the fairing's air loads into the tank wall. Avionics boxes, batteries and the cold-gas thrusters are packed around its inside.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m in diameter, matching the stage
Roughly 1 m tall
Carries the satellite and fairing, typically several tonnes
details.madeOf: Aluminium or carbon-composite skin with internal ribs, painted white to reflect sunlight and keep the electronics cool.

parts.name: Forward skirt

parts.description: Triple-redundant computer that steers the upper stage into orbit.

details.didYouKnow: Triple voting is an old trick: the Space Shuttle went further and flew with five main flight computers.
details.howItWorks: The flight computers read gyroscopes, accelerometers and GPS to know exactly where the stage is and how fast it is moving, then command the engine gimbal and thrusters to follow the planned path. Three independent units vote on every decision, so a single faulty computer is simply outvoted. They also time engine cut-off, coast phases and satellite release.
keyNumbers: Three redundant units
Recalculate the trajectory many times a second
Guide the stage to orbit within roughly a few kilometres of target
details.madeOf: Circuit boards in sealed aluminium boxes with plastic-and-metal connectors. Some rockets like this use ordinary commercial processors made reliable by redundancy rather than expensive radiation-hardened chips.

parts.name: Upper-stage flight computer

parts.description: Cold-gas thrusters that orient the stage while coasting in space.

details.didYouKnow: Cold gas is used because it is simple and safe: nothing burns, so the thrusters can fire thousands of times without wearing out.
details.howItWorks: When the main engine is off, the stage has nothing to steer with, so these pods puff nitrogen gas through small nozzles to turn it. They point the stage for burns, hold it steady for satellite release, and give a gentle push to settle the propellant at the bottom of the tanks before the engine relights. Opposing pods can roll, pitch or yaw the stage.
keyNumbers: Each thruster gives roughly tens of newtons
Nitrogen stored at up to about 300 bar
Two pods, one on each side
details.madeOf: Aluminium housings with small stainless-steel valves and nozzles, fed by a carbon-overwrapped nitrogen bottle.

parts.name: Nitrogen thruster pod

parts.description: Pressure dome that closes the top of the kerosene tank.

details.didYouKnow: Friction-stir welding joins metal by stirring it with a spinning tool without melting it, giving stronger seams than conventional welding.
details.howItWorks: A dome is the natural shape for holding pressure, spreading the force evenly so the metal can be thin. This one seals the top of the fuel tank and has ports where helium enters to keep the tank pressurised and sensors check the level. It also passes loads from the forward skirt into the tank barrel.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m across
Holds a pressure of roughly 2 to 3 bar
Metal only a few millimetres thick
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy gores, often spun or formed and then friction-stir welded together. The alloy is lighter and stronger than ordinary aluminium.

parts.name: Fuel tank upper dome

parts.description: Aluminium-lithium barrel holding the kerosene (RP-1) for the vacuum engine.

details.didYouKnow: RP-1 is a highly refined kerosene, similar to jet fuel but with tighter limits on sulphur and other impurities that could clog the engine.
details.howItWorks: This barrel holds the upper stage's kerosene, which flows down a pipe through the oxygen tank to the engine. As fuel drains out, helium is fed in at the top so the pressure stays steady and the pump inlet never starves. The tank wall is also the stage's main structure, carrying thrust from below and the payload from above.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 30 tonnes of kerosene
About 3.7 m in diameter
Fuel chilled to about minus 7 °C to make it denser
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy sheet, machined thin in places and friction-stir welded into a cylinder. Being both container and structure saves a lot of mass.

parts.name: Upper-stage fuel tank

parts.description: Single insulated dome that separates the fuel above from the super-cold oxygen below, saving length and mass.

details.didYouKnow: The Apollo-era Saturn V upper stages used common bulkheads too, making them some of the lightest large stages ever flown.
details.howItWorks: Instead of two separate tanks with a gap between them, one shared dome divides kerosene from liquid oxygen. That shortens and lightens the stage, but the dome must cope with a big temperature difference on its two faces and with pressure pushing from either side. Insulation stops the oxygen from freezing the kerosene.
keyNumbers: Separates liquids roughly 200 °C apart
About 3.7 m across
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy, sometimes with an insulating layer or a double-walled construction to limit heat flow between the propellants.

parts.name: Common bulkhead

parts.description: Barrel holding liquid oxygen chilled to −207 °C.

details.didYouKnow: Chilling oxygen below its normal boiling point makes it denser, letting the same tank hold several percent more propellant.
details.howItWorks: Liquid oxygen is the oxidiser: kerosene cannot burn in space without it, and the engine uses more than twice as much oxygen as fuel by mass. The tank sits below the fuel and feeds the engine through its lower dome. Its super-chilled contents are loaded shortly before launch because they slowly boil off.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 75 tonnes of liquid oxygen
Oxygen chilled to about minus 207 °C
Oxygen-to-fuel ratio about 2.3 to 1 by mass
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy, which actually gets stronger at very low temperatures, making it a good match for cryogenic propellant.

parts.name: Upper-stage oxygen tank

parts.description: Bottom dome of the oxygen tank; the engine feed line leaves from its centre.

details.didYouKnow: If gas bubbles reach a turbopump spinning at tens of thousands of rpm, it can lose grip on the liquid and fail in a fraction of a second.
details.howItWorks: This dome closes the base of the oxygen tank and funnels liquid to an outlet at its centre, which leads straight to the engine's turbopump. Devices near the outlet stop swirling and vortexes, like the whirlpool in a draining bath, which could let gas bubbles into the pump. The thrust cone attaches around its outside.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m across
Drains roughly 200 kg of oxygen per second at full thrust
Holds tank pressure of a few bar
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy formed into a dome and welded to the tank barrel.

parts.name: Oxygen tank lower dome

parts.description: Carbon-overwrapped tank of high-pressure helium that keeps the propellant tanks pressurised as they drain.

details.didYouKnow: Helium is used even though it is expensive because almost any other gas would either liquefy or react at liquid-oxygen temperatures.
details.howItWorks: As propellant drains, something must fill the space so the tanks keep their pressure and shape; helium from these bottles does that. It is light, does not react with anything and stays a gas even at extreme cold. A regulator steps its very high storage pressure down to the gentle pressure the tanks need.
keyNumbers: Store helium at up to about 400 bar
Weigh far less than an all-metal bottle of the same capacity
Usually about 1 m long or less
details.madeOf: A thin metal liner, often aluminium or titanium, wound with many layers of carbon fibre in resin. COPV stands for composite overwrapped pressure vessel.

parts.name: Helium pressurant bottle

parts.description: Conical structure that passes the engine's push into the tanks.

details.didYouKnow: Thrust from a single engine at the back is what actually lifts the stage: the whole structure is effectively being pushed up from below, not pulled.
details.howItWorks: The engine pushes at a single point, but the tanks need that force spread evenly around their rim. This cone collects the push from the engine's gimbal mount and fans it out to the base of the oxygen tank wall. It also carries the engine's steering actuators and plumbing.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 1,000 kilonewtons of thrust
Spreads the load over a ring about 3.7 m across
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy with stiffening rings and stringers, machined to be strong along the load paths and thin everywhere else.

parts.name: Thrust cone

parts.description: Huge thin niobium bell that expands exhaust in near-vacuum; it glows cherry red in flight.

details.didYouKnow: Because it is uncooled, the bell can be seen glowing orange-red in onboard camera views as the upper stage climbs to orbit.
details.howItWorks: The longer and wider a nozzle is, the more it can expand the exhaust and squeeze thrust from it, but at sea level the air would push back on such a big bell. In near vacuum there is no such problem, so this extension is enormous. It has no cooling channels: it simply radiates its heat away and glows.
keyNumbers: Exit roughly 3 m across
Expands the gas about 165 times by area
Glows at roughly 1,000 °C or more
details.madeOf: A niobium alloy, which keeps its strength at very high temperatures and is coated to resist oxidation. It is only about as thick as a few sheets of card.

parts.name: Nozzle extension

parts.description: Copper-lined chamber where kerosene and oxygen burn at ~3,300 °C, cooled by fuel flowing through its walls.

details.didYouKnow: The copper wall stays cool enough to survive only because fuel is rushing through channels just millimetres away from the flame.
details.howItWorks: This is where the propellants burn, at a pressure of nearly a hundred atmospheres, before the gas squeezes through the narrow throat and expands into the nozzle. The flame is hotter than the melting point of copper, so fuel is first pumped through channels in the walls to carry heat away before it is burned. This trick is called regenerative cooling.
keyNumbers: Combustion gas reaches about 3,300 °C
Chamber pressure roughly 100 bar
The engine fires for about 6 minutes on a typical mission
details.madeOf: A copper alloy inner liner, chosen because it conducts heat superbly, with a stronger nickel or steel outer jacket to hold the pressure.

parts.name: Combustion chamber

parts.description: Gas turbine spinning at ~36,000 rpm that drives the fuel and oxygen pumps.

details.didYouKnow: A turbopump smaller than a microwave oven can move enough propellant to fill a bathtub every second or so.
details.howItWorks: A small gas generator burns some propellant to spin a turbine, which drives the fuel and oxygen pumps on a shared shaft. The pumps raise propellant from a few bar in the tanks to well over a hundred bar so it can be forced into the chamber. This layout, where the turbine gas is dumped rather than burned again, is called an open cycle.
keyNumbers: Spins at about 36,000 rpm
Turbine produces a few megawatts of power
Weighs only tens of kilograms
details.madeOf: High-strength steels and nickel superalloys for the turbine, with special bearings and seals to keep the hot gas, the kerosene and the oxygen from ever meeting where they should not.

parts.name: Turbopump

parts.description: Routes the turbine's spent gas overboard.

details.didYouKnow: Kerosene-burning gas generators run fuel-rich to keep the turbine from melting, which is why their exhaust is dark and smoky.
details.howItWorks: After spinning the turbine, the gas generator's fuel-rich exhaust still has to go somewhere. This duct carries it away from the turbine and dumps it overboard, often into the nozzle extension where it helps form a cooler protective layer on the wall. The dumped gas still adds a small amount of thrust.
keyNumbers: Carries a few percent of the engine's propellant flow
Gas at several hundred °C
Adds a small fraction of total thrust
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant steel or nickel alloy tubing, able to handle hot, sooty gas for minutes at a time.

parts.name: Turbine exhaust duct

parts.description: Sprays propellants into the chamber; the gimbal on top lets the engine swivel to steer.

details.didYouKnow: The engine is lit with a squirt of chemicals that burst into flame on contact with air, giving a brief bright green flash at ignition.
details.howItWorks: The injector is a plate drilled with many precisely aimed holes that spray fuel and oxygen so they collide, atomise and mix evenly, much like a shower head. In rockets like this a central pintle design is often used, spraying a sheet of one propellant through a ring of the other. Above it, the gimbal joint lets actuators tilt the whole engine a few degrees to steer the stage.
keyNumbers: Gimbals up to about 5 degrees
Carries roughly 1,000 kilonewtons of thrust
Can be relit several times in one mission
details.madeOf: Precision-machined stainless steel or nickel alloy for the injector, with a forged steel or titanium gimbal block that carries the full engine thrust.

parts.name: Injector head & gimbal

parts.description: Carbon-composite shell that joins the stages and hides the vacuum engine until separation.

details.didYouKnow: Because the interstage stays on the booster, it also becomes the mounting point for the grid fins used on the way home.
details.howItWorks: The interstage is a hollow sleeve on top of the booster that covers the upper-stage engine and connects the two stages structurally. During ascent it carries the full weight and thrust load between them. At separation, latches release and the upper stage's engine slides out of it before lighting.
keyNumbers: Roughly 6 to 7 m long
About 3.7 m in diameter
Stays attached to the booster and returns with it
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre over an aluminium honeycomb core, usually painted black. It is light but stiff enough to carry the upper stage and payload.

parts.name: Interstage

parts.description: Titanium lattice fin that unfolds on the way back down to steer the booster to its landing pad.

details.didYouKnow: Grid fins were first used on Soviet missiles and on the escape system of the Soyuz crew capsule before being used to land boosters.
details.howItWorks: During ascent the fins lie folded against the interstage. On the way back down they swing out and, as the booster falls through the air backwards, tilting them steers it like the flaps on an aircraft. The lattice of small cells works well across a huge range of speeds, from supersonic to slow, and folds compactly.
keyNumbers: Each about 1.5 m across
Each weighs a few hundred kilograms
Steer the booster to a landing within a few metres
details.madeOf: Cast and machined titanium, which survives the heating of re-entry without needing paint or coatings that would burn off. Earlier aluminium versions charred and had to be replaced.

parts.name: Grid fin

parts.description: Hydraulic drive that rotates its grid fin.

details.didYouKnow: On an early landing attempt the booster ran out of hydraulic fluid just before touchdown, lost steering and crashed, so the reservoir was enlarged.
details.howItWorks: Each actuator first unfolds its fin, then twists it back and forth to steer during descent. On rockets like this the hydraulics are an open-loop system, using pressurised fluid that is vented overboard after use rather than pumped back. That saves weight because the booster only needs the fins for a few minutes.
keyNumbers: Four actuators, one per fin
Turns its fin through roughly tens of degrees
Only needed for a few minutes per flight
details.madeOf: Steel and aluminium hydraulic cylinders and valves, driven by pressurised fluid from a small reservoir.

parts.name: Grid fin actuator

parts.description: Nitrogen thrusters that flip the booster around after separation.

details.didYouKnow: The puffs of white gas you sometimes see from a returning booster's top in launch videos are these thrusters firing.
details.howItWorks: Right after separation the booster is high above most of the air, so fins are useless. These pods fire jets of nitrogen to flip the booster round to point engines-first for its return burns, and to hold it steady while it coasts. They sit near the top of the booster, where they have the most leverage.
keyNumbers: Turns a booster roughly 45 m long end over end
Flip completed in roughly 10 to 20 seconds
Nitrogen stored at up to about 300 bar
details.madeOf: Aluminium housings and stainless-steel valves fed by carbon-overwrapped nitrogen bottles.

parts.name: Cold-gas thruster pack

parts.description: Pneumatic piston that shoves the upper stage clear of the booster.

details.didYouKnow: At separation the rocket is roughly 60 to 80 km high, already above more than 99 percent of the atmosphere by mass.
details.howItWorks: Once the booster's engines shut down and the latches between the stages release, these pistons push the upper stage gently away. The push opens a gap so the upper-stage engine can light without blasting the booster. Pneumatic pushers can be reset and reused, unlike explosive bolts.
keyNumbers: Separation happens about 2.5 minutes after liftoff
Stages part at roughly 2 km/s
Upper engine lights a few seconds later
details.madeOf: Steel pistons and cylinders driven by pressurised helium or nitrogen.

parts.name: Separation pusher

parts.description: Guides the booster up, then back down to a pinpoint landing.

details.didYouKnow: The landing burn is a hoverslam: the booster cannot hover, so the engine must reach zero speed at exactly zero height.
details.howItWorks: On the way up, these computers fly the booster on the planned path and manage the nine engines. After separation they take over a completely different job: plotting the flip, the boost-back, re-entry and landing burns in real time. The landing burn is calculated to bring the booster to zero speed just as the legs touch.
keyNumbers: Land the booster within a few metres of target
Landing burn lasts about 30 seconds
Guide a return trip of up to several hundred kilometres
details.madeOf: Electronics in sealed aluminium boxes, using redundant processors and sensors including GPS and inertial measurement units.

parts.name: Booster flight computer

parts.description: Top dome of the booster's oxygen tank.

details.didYouKnow: A pressurised tank is much stiffer than an empty one, a little like an inflated balloon compared to a flat one.
details.howItWorks: This dome caps the top of the booster's oxygen tank and takes the internal pressure. Helium pressurisation lines and level sensors enter through it. Its rim joins the tank barrel to the interstage, so it also carries the upper stage's weight into the booster.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m across
Holds a pressure of roughly 3 bar
Metal just a few millimetres thick
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy, formed and friction-stir welded. The alloy combines low weight with good strength at cryogenic temperatures.

parts.name: Oxygen tank upper dome

parts.description: 22 m aluminium-lithium barrel of liquid oxygen — the largest single part of the rocket.

details.didYouKnow: Frost and ice often form on the outside of the tank during fuelling as moisture in the air freezes against the super-cold wall.
details.howItWorks: This tank holds the oxygen the nine engines need to burn their kerosene. It sits above the fuel tank, and the oxygen reaches the engines through the downcomer pipe running through the fuel. Kept under pressure, the tank wall is also the main backbone of the booster.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 280 tonnes of liquid oxygen
Oxygen chilled to about minus 207 °C
About 3.7 m wide
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy panels friction-stir welded into a cylinder. Rockets like this make the tank walls do double duty as structure to keep weight down.

parts.name: Booster oxygen tank

parts.description: Ring that damps propellant sloshing, which could otherwise upset the rocket's steering.

details.didYouKnow: Slosh is a real hazard: uncontrolled sloshing has contributed to the loss of rockets in the past.
details.howItWorks: As the rocket steers and vibrates, liquid in a tank can slosh from side to side, and that moving mass can push the rocket off course or fight the steering system. This top baffle sits near the upper part of the tank, where it calms the liquid early in flight when the tank is nearly full. It works like a ring-shaped shelf that breaks up waves.
keyNumbers: Ring a few tens of centimetres deep
Fits inside a tank about 3.7 m wide
Weighs only a few kilograms
details.madeOf: Aluminium sheet or rings riveted or welded to the tank wall, light enough not to cost much payload.

parts.name: Oxygen slosh baffle 1

parts.description: Ring that damps propellant sloshing, which could otherwise upset the rocket's steering.

details.didYouKnow: Engineers model slosh as a pendulum hidden inside the tank, and its swing rate changes as the tank empties.
details.howItWorks: This middle baffle takes over as the liquid level drops in the middle part of the flight. Sloshing is strongest when the liquid surface is near a baffle, so spacing several of them up the tank keeps damping effective all the way through the burn. It also stiffens the tank wall slightly.
keyNumbers: One of three oxygen baffles
Tank drains roughly 1.8 tonnes of oxygen per second
Positioned roughly mid-way down the tank
details.madeOf: Lightweight aluminium alloy, matching the tank wall to avoid corrosion where different metals touch.

parts.name: Oxygen slosh baffle 2

parts.description: Ring that damps propellant sloshing, which could otherwise upset the rocket's steering.

details.didYouKnow: A reusable booster has to save a few percent of its propellant to land, which makes keeping those last tonnes calm especially important.
details.howItWorks: The lowest baffle calms the liquid late in the burn, when the tank is nearly empty and the rocket is accelerating hardest. It also matters on the way home, when a small amount of leftover oxygen must stay settled for the booster's relights. Calm liquid at the bottom means a steady flow into the downcomer.
keyNumbers: Sits a few metres above the lower dome
Works under acceleration of up to about 4 g
One of three oxygen baffles
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy rings with cut-outs to let liquid drain through while still breaking up waves.

parts.name: Oxygen slosh baffle 3

parts.description: Carbon-overwrapped helium bottle submerged in the oxygen for extra-dense storage.

details.didYouKnow: Mounting these bottles inside liquid oxygen is tricky: a failure of one during fuelling once destroyed a rocket of this type on the pad.
details.howItWorks: These bottles supply helium that keeps both booster tanks pressurised as they drain. Submerging them in the super-cold oxygen shrinks the helium so much more of it fits in each bottle. Before release to the tanks the helium is warmed, which makes it expand and stretch further.
keyNumbers: Store helium at up to about 400 bar
Immersed in oxygen at about minus 207 °C
Usually several bottles in the tank
details.madeOf: A thin metal liner wrapped in carbon fibre and resin, which resists bursting at high pressure for a fraction of the weight of steel.

parts.name: Helium pressurant bottle

parts.description: Bottom dome of the oxygen tank; the downcomer drains through its centre.

details.didYouKnow: At liftoff the liquid above this dome weighs about as much as two blue whales.
details.howItWorks: This dome closes the bottom of the oxygen tank and funnels oxygen into the downcomer at its centre. A curved dome is used because it spreads the tank pressure and the weight of liquid above it evenly. Below it lies the intertank ring and then the top of the fuel tank.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m across
Supports roughly 280 tonnes of oxygen at liftoff
Feeds about 1.8 tonnes of oxygen per second
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy, formed into a dome and friction-stir welded to the tank barrel.

parts.name: Oxygen tank lower dome

parts.description: Short structural ring between the two booster tanks.

details.didYouKnow: On many rockets the intertank is also where the umbilical lines from the launch tower connect.
details.howItWorks: The intertank is a short, unpressurised ring that joins the oxygen tank above to the fuel tank below. It carries all the thrust and weight loads between the two tanks and gives room for the domes to bulge into. Some rockets of this type use a common bulkhead instead, but a separate ring keeps the propellants well apart.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m in diameter
Roughly 1 to 2 m tall
Carries several meganewtons of thrust load
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy with stiffening stringers and rings, since it has no internal pressure to help hold its shape.

parts.name: Intertank ring

parts.description: Top dome of the kerosene tank.

details.didYouKnow: Kerosene is less dense than oxygen, so the fuel tank must be relatively large even though the engines burn much less fuel than oxygen by mass.
details.howItWorks: This dome seals the top of the kerosene tank, facing the oxygen tank's lower dome across the intertank. The downcomer passes straight through its centre with a sealed joint. Helium for pressurisation enters through a port near its top.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m across
Holds tank pressure of roughly 2 to 3 bar
Pierced by an oxygen pipe about 0.5 m wide
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy, formed and welded like the other domes so the whole booster shares the same welding process.

parts.name: Fuel tank upper dome

parts.description: 15 m barrel of rocket-grade kerosene (RP-1).

details.didYouKnow: Kerosene used to be shipped to launch sites in ordinary tanker trucks, as it is far easier to handle than liquid hydrogen.
details.howItWorks: This barrel holds the kerosene for all nine booster engines, with the downcomer passing through its middle. Fuel flows out of the lower dome to each engine's turbopump, and some of it first cools the engine walls before burning. Like the oxygen tank above, it is kept pressurised and also forms part of the booster's structure.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 120 tonnes of kerosene
About 3.7 m wide
Fuel chilled to roughly minus 7 °C to pack more in
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy friction-stir welded into a cylinder, with internal stiffening rings.

parts.name: Booster fuel tank

parts.description: Ring that damps kerosene sloshing.

details.didYouKnow: Even a small shift in fuel position matters, because a fully loaded booster tank holds about a hundred tonnes of kerosene.
details.howItWorks: This upper baffle damps sloshing kerosene while the fuel tank is still fairly full, early in flight. Sloshing liquid shifts the rocket's balance and can resonate with the steering system, so damping it keeps control smooth. It is shaped to clear the downcomer running down the middle of the tank.
keyNumbers: One of two fuel baffles
Inside a tank about 15 m long
Weighs only a few kilograms
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy rings or perforated sheet attached to the tank wall.

parts.name: Fuel slosh baffle 1

parts.description: Ring that damps kerosene sloshing.

details.didYouKnow: When the engines cut off, the propellants can float up off the bottom of the tank, so they must be settled again before each relight.
details.howItWorks: The lower fuel baffle calms the kerosene as the tank nears empty, and keeps the last few tonnes settled for the booster's boost-back, re-entry and landing burns. Steady liquid near the outlets stops gas being drawn into the feed lines. It also helps after engine cut-off, when liquid can surge upwards.
keyNumbers: Sits a few metres above the lower dome
Fuel flow to the engines about 800 kg per second
One of two fuel baffles
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy, with openings to let fuel drain freely while breaking up waves.

parts.name: Fuel slosh baffle 2

parts.description: Wide pipe that carries oxygen straight down through the fuel tank to the engines.

details.didYouKnow: The kerosene around the pipe is chilled too, which helps stop it warming the oxygen on the way down.
details.howItWorks: Because the oxygen tank sits on top, its oxygen has to get past the fuel tank to reach the engines. The downcomer is a straight, wide pipe running down the centre of the fuel tank to the engine bay. Running it inside the tank keeps the outside of the booster smooth and the pipe short.
keyNumbers: Roughly 0.5 m in diameter
About 15 m long
Carries about 1.8 tonnes of oxygen per second
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy tubing with insulation and flexible joints, since the super-cold pipe shrinks relative to the warmer fuel tank around it.

parts.name: Oxygen downcomer

parts.description: Bottom dome of the kerosene tank; feed lines to all nine engines leave here.

details.didYouKnow: Every pipe connection through the dome is a possible leak point, so each one is pressure tested before flight.
details.howItWorks: This dome forms the floor of the fuel tank and the roof of the engine bay. Feed lines to all nine engines leave from it, and the downcomer passes through to an oxygen manifold below. It also connects to the thrust structure, so the engines' push enters the tanks here.
keyNumbers: About 3.7 m across
Has nine fuel outlets, one per engine
Supports roughly 120 tonnes of kerosene at liftoff
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy formed into a dome, reinforced around the many pipe outlets.

parts.name: Fuel tank lower dome

parts.description: Fairing along the outside of the tanks that carries wiring and pressurisation lines between the engine bay and interstage.

details.didYouKnow: The raceway is one of the few things that breaks up the smooth cylinder of the booster, and it can be seen as a stripe running down the side.
details.howItWorks: The raceway is a covered channel running along the outside of the booster. It protects the wiring, data cables and pressurisation lines that link the computers at the top with the engines at the bottom. Putting them outside the tanks keeps them away from the super-cold propellants and makes them easy to inspect.
keyNumbers: Runs roughly 35 m along the booster
Only a few tens of centimetres wide
details.madeOf: Aluminium or composite cover panels over brackets, often with insulation to protect the cables from heat and cold.

parts.name: Cable raceway

parts.description: Carbon-fibre and aluminium-honeycomb leg, stowed flat on ascent and swung down for touchdown.

details.didYouKnow: The legs add a couple of tonnes to the booster, which is one reason rockets like this carry slightly less to orbit when they are recovered.
details.howItWorks: During ascent each leg folds flat against the booster's side to stay out of the airflow. Just before landing it swings down and locks, and the four legs together form a wide, stable base. A leg also takes the impact of touchdown together with its piston.
keyNumbers: About 18 m span when all four are out
Each leg weighs roughly 500 kg to 600 kg
Deploy in a few seconds before touchdown
details.madeOf: Carbon-fibre skins over an aluminium honeycomb core, which gives a long, stiff leg at a low weight.

parts.name: Landing leg

parts.description: Telescoping pneumatic strut that pushes its leg out and absorbs the landing shock.

details.didYouKnow: Landing a booster on four legs is often compared to balancing a tall pencil upright on a moving boat in a storm.
details.howItWorks: When it is time to land, high-pressure helium pushes this telescoping strut out, swinging the leg down until it locks. On touchdown the piston compresses to absorb the shock. Gravity and air resistance help the leg fall into place too.
keyNumbers: Swings its leg out in a matter of seconds
Absorbs a touchdown at roughly 2 m/s or less
Four pistons, one per leg
details.madeOf: Steel and aluminium telescoping cylinders, with crushable or damping elements that soak up energy at landing.

parts.name: Leg deployment piston

parts.description: Crushable pad at the tip of each leg.

details.didYouKnow: The Apollo lunar module landing legs also used crushable aluminium honeycomb to absorb the touchdown.
details.howItWorks: Each pad spreads the leg's load on the landing surface and contains a crushable honeycomb core that flattens to soak up energy. The pad is replaced or refurbished if it crushes. Its wide footprint also stops the leg digging into the deck of a landing ship.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1 m across
Four pads in total
Shares a landing load of roughly 25 tonnes of booster
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel shell with an aluminium honeycomb crush core, which absorbs energy predictably as it collapses.

parts.name: Foot pad

parts.description: Outer shell of the engine bay; the whole rocket stands on it at the launch pad.

details.didYouKnow: The hold-down clamps can keep the rocket pinned while the engines are running and shut them down if anything looks wrong.
details.howItWorks: The aft skirt is the outer shell around the engines at the bottom of the booster. On the launch pad, the whole fuelled rocket rests on hold-down clamps attached to it, which only release once all engines are confirmed healthy. The landing legs are also hinged from its sides.
keyNumbers: Carries the weight of about 550 tonnes on the pad
Holds the rocket down for about 3 seconds after ignition
About 3.7 m in diameter
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy with heavy stiffening to carry the rocket's weight on the pad and the landing-leg loads.

parts.name: Aft skirt

parts.description: Octagonal structure that bolts all nine engines to the booster and carries their combined push.

details.didYouKnow: The name comes from its eight-sided web shape, which matches the ring of eight outer engines.
details.howItWorks: The octaweb is the frame the nine engines bolt to, eight around the outside and one in the middle. It gathers their combined push and transfers it to the fuel tank above. Its compact layout lets the booster lose an engine and still keep the thrust balanced.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 7,600 kilonewtons of thrust at liftoff
Supports nine engines
About 3.7 m across
details.madeOf: Machined and welded aluminium beams and plates, which are light enough for a reusable booster yet very strong.

parts.name: Octaweb thrust plate

parts.description: Radial beam of the octaweb between two engines.

details.didYouKnow: Because the booster flies many times, beams like this are inspected for cracks between flights, much like aircraft parts.
details.howItWorks: Each beam runs from the centre outwards between two outer engines, tying the frame together like spokes of a wheel. It shares the thrust from neighbouring engines and keeps the frame stiff so the engines stay aligned. Plumbing and wiring can be routed along it to each engine.
keyNumbers: One of eight radial beams
Shares loads from engines each making about 850 kilonewtons
Roughly 1.5 m long
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy, machined from solid billet or built up from plates, chosen for a good strength-to-weight ratio.

parts.name: Octaweb beam

parts.description: Ceramic blanket that protects the engine bay from the heat of the exhaust plume.

details.didYouKnow: The reusable booster's base comes back scorched and sooty, and the heat shield is one of the parts most often refurbished.
details.howItWorks: Nine engines firing side by side create intense heat, and some of the hot gas can swirl back towards the engine bay. This shield covers the base with heat-resistant blankets, with flexible boots around each engine so they can still swivel. It is especially important on re-entry, when the booster falls engines-first into the plume of its own burn.
keyNumbers: Withstands temperatures of over 1,000 °C
Covers a base about 3.7 m wide
Has nine openings for the engines
details.madeOf: Ceramic fibre blankets and tiles, sometimes over a metal backing, which insulate well and survive temperatures over 1,000 °C.

parts.name: Engine heat shield

parts.description: Bell-shaped nozzle that accelerates exhaust to about 3 km/s.

details.didYouKnow: On the way down, only some of these engines relight, because nine engines would be far too much thrust for a nearly empty booster.
details.howItWorks: The bell shape turns hot, high-pressure gas into a fast jet, and the faster the exhaust leaves, the more thrust each kilogram of propellant gives. The outer engines are arranged in a ring so the booster can steer by tilting them. Their nozzles are shorter than the vacuum engine's because air at sea level pushes back on a large bell.
keyNumbers: Eight outer engines
Exit about 1 m across
Each engine makes roughly 850 kilonewtons at sea level
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant steel or nickel alloy, partly cooled by fuel running through its walls and partly by a layer of turbine exhaust.

parts.name: Outer engine nozzle

parts.description: Regeneratively cooled copper chamber where propellants burn.

details.didYouKnow: Engines of this type can be flown more than 20 times before being retired, a record that was unthinkable for rockets only a decade or two ago.
details.howItWorks: Inside, kerosene and oxygen burn at high pressure, creating the hot gas that leaves through the nozzle. The chamber walls are cooled by fuel flowing through channels before it is injected, otherwise they would melt in seconds. Each outer engine relights several times on a reusable flight.
keyNumbers: Combustion pressure roughly 100 bar
Gas at about 3,300 °C
Fires for roughly 160 seconds on ascent
details.madeOf: A copper alloy liner, for its excellent heat conduction, inside an outer jacket of stronger nickel or steel to hold the pressure.

parts.name: Outer engine combustion chamber

parts.description: Ring that feeds kerosene into the chamber's cooling channels.

details.didYouKnow: Some engines use the warm fuel from the cooling channels to drive the turbopump, but open-cycle engines like these send it to the injector instead.
details.howItWorks: The manifold is a ring-shaped pipe that collects kerosene from the turbopump and spreads it evenly into hundreds of tiny cooling channels in the chamber wall. The fuel soaks up heat as it flows, then goes on to the injector to be burned. Even distribution is vital, since one starved channel could create a hot spot.
keyNumbers: Feeds roughly 100 or more cooling channels
Fuel flows at over 100 bar
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or nickel alloy tubing, welded or brazed to the chamber, which must take high pressure and temperature differences.

parts.name: Outer engine cooling manifold

parts.description: Mixes the propellants; the gimbal block lets the engine swivel a few degrees to steer.

details.didYouKnow: Pintle injectors were developed for the Apollo lunar module descent engine because they resist combustion instability, which can wreck an engine.
details.howItWorks: The injector sprays fuel and oxygen into the chamber so they mix finely and burn evenly. Engines like this commonly use a pintle injector, a central post that sprays a sheet of propellant into a ring of the other. The gimbal joint above lets each outer engine tilt a few degrees, so together they can steer pitch, yaw and roll.
keyNumbers: Gimbals up to about 5 degrees
Carries roughly 850 kilonewtons
Eight outer injectors
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or nickel alloy machined to tight tolerances, with a forged gimbal block that carries the engine's full thrust.

parts.name: Outer engine injector & gimbal

parts.description: Turbine-driven pumps that force ~300 kg of propellant per second into the chamber.

details.didYouKnow: The combined turbopumps of all nine engines can produce tens of megawatts, comparable to a small power station.
details.howItWorks: A gas generator burns a little propellant to spin a turbine, which drives pumps for both fuel and oxygen on a shared shaft. The pumps raise the propellant to high pressure so it can be forced into the combustion chamber. Each outer engine has its own turbopump, so one failing does not affect the others.
keyNumbers: Moves about 300 kg of propellant per second
Spins at about 36,000 rpm
Produces several megawatts of power
details.madeOf: High-strength steel and nickel superalloys for the turbine and pump wheels, with precision bearings that run in cryogenic oxygen.

parts.name: Outer engine turbopump

parts.description: Dumps the turbine's sooty exhaust beside the nozzle.

details.didYouKnow: The black soot that covers a returning booster comes partly from these turbine exhausts.
details.howItWorks: This pipe carries the spent, fuel-rich gas from the turbine and dumps it beside the nozzle. Because it is rich in fuel, it burns or smokes in the plume, giving a dark streak in the exhaust. The dumped gas adds a little thrust but is mainly a way to get rid of it.
keyNumbers: Gas at several hundred °C
Carries a few percent of the engine's propellant
Eight outer exhaust pipes
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant steel or nickel alloy tubing able to take hot gas for minutes.

parts.name: Outer engine turbine exhaust

parts.description: Hydraulic ram that tilts the engine on its gimbal.

details.didYouKnow: Using rocket fuel as hydraulic fluid saves the weight of a separate hydraulic supply, an idea that goes back to the Saturn V.
details.howItWorks: Two actuators per engine push and pull at right angles to tilt it on its gimbal, steering the rocket like the rudder of a boat. The flight computer commands them many times a second. On the booster, the hydraulic system is powered by the kerosene itself, pressurised by the turbopump.
keyNumbers: Tilts the engine up to about 5 degrees
Responds in fractions of a second
Pushes with forces of tens of kilonewtons
details.madeOf: Steel hydraulic cylinders and valves, built to handle large forces quickly and precisely.

parts.name: Outer engine steering actuator

parts.description: Duct carrying kerosene from the tank to the turbopump.

details.didYouKnow: Each engine also needs its own oxygen line, branching from a manifold at the bottom of the downcomer.
details.howItWorks: This duct takes kerosene from the bottom of the fuel tank to the turbopump of an outer engine. It must stay flexible enough to let the engine gimbal and to cope with vibration. Valves close it when the engine shuts down.
keyNumbers: Carries about 90 kg of fuel per second
Roughly 10 to 15 cm in diameter
Eight outer fuel lines
details.madeOf: Aluminium or stainless-steel tubing, with flexible bellows joints to allow movement.

parts.name: Outer engine fuel feed line

parts.description: Bell-shaped nozzle that accelerates exhaust to about 3 km/s.

details.didYouKnow: Because even one engine at its lowest setting is too strong to hover the empty booster, the landing burn must be timed perfectly.
details.howItWorks: The centre engine's nozzle is the same design as the outer ones, but this engine plays a special role on the way home. For the final landing burn the booster often uses only this single centre engine, which gives a precise, centred thrust to touch down. A single engine still makes more thrust than the empty booster weighs.
keyNumbers: Exit about 1 m across
Exhaust leaves at about 3 km/s
Relit up to about three times per flight
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant steel or nickel alloy, partly cooled by fuel and partly by turbine exhaust.

parts.name: Centre engine nozzle

parts.description: Regeneratively cooled copper chamber where propellants burn.

details.didYouKnow: The ability to throttle the engine down is essential for landing, as it controls how fast the booster slows.
details.howItWorks: This chamber is where the centre engine burns its propellants, like the outer ones. The centre engine fires on ascent and is the one most often used for landing, so it is relit more times than most of the others. Its walls are cooled by kerosene flowing through channels before injection.
keyNumbers: About 3,300 °C gas
Roughly 100 bar chamber pressure
Can throttle down to roughly 40 percent thrust or so
details.madeOf: Copper alloy liner inside a stronger nickel or steel jacket.

parts.name: Centre engine combustion chamber

parts.description: Ring that feeds kerosene into the chamber's cooling channels.

details.didYouKnow: Each time an engine starts and stops, the metal expands and contracts, and those cycles are one of the main limits on how many times it can fly.
details.howItWorks: Just like on the outer engines, this ring feeds kerosene into the cooling channels of the chamber. Because the centre engine fires the most often during a reusable flight, its cooling system sees the most heat cycles. Even fuel distribution prevents hot spots during the repeated restarts.
keyNumbers: Feeds roughly 100 or more cooling channels
Fuel pressure over 100 bar
Heated and cooled several times per flight
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or nickel alloy, brazed or welded to the chamber.

parts.name: Centre engine cooling manifold

parts.description: Mixes the propellants; the gimbal block lets the engine swivel a few degrees to steer.

details.didYouKnow: The centre engine sits right on the booster's axis, so when it fires straight it pushes without twisting the booster at all, which makes it ideal for landing.
details.howItWorks: The centre injector mixes fuel and oxygen just like the outer ones. Its gimbal is used mostly during landing, where it steers the booster precisely over the pad on a single engine. The gimbal also allows the centre engine to help with steering on ascent.
keyNumbers: Gimbals up to about 5 degrees
Carries roughly 850 kilonewtons
Relit up to about three times per flight
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or nickel alloy injector with a forged steel gimbal block.

parts.name: Centre engine injector & gimbal

parts.description: Turbine-driven pumps that force ~300 kg of propellant per second into the chamber.

details.didYouKnow: A turbopump that has to restart in flight is much harder to design than one that only starts on the ground, where helpers can spin it up.
details.howItWorks: This turbopump drives the centre engine, pumping propellant into the chamber at high pressure. It must restart reliably several times in one flight, spinning up from rest in a second or two. The landing depends on it working perfectly on the final relight.
keyNumbers: Spins at about 36,000 rpm
Moves about 300 kg of propellant per second
Spins up in about a second or two
details.madeOf: High-strength steel and nickel superalloys, with bearings that work in liquid oxygen.

parts.name: Centre engine turbopump

parts.description: Dumps the turbine's sooty exhaust beside the nozzle.

details.didYouKnow: The dark, sooty exhaust from turbine pipes is a big reason kerosene boosters need cleaning between flights.
details.howItWorks: This duct dumps the centre engine's turbine gas into the plume. Because the centre engine is surrounded by the eight outer engines, its exhaust duct must be routed carefully between them. It adds a little thrust as it leaves.
keyNumbers: Gas at several hundred °C
Carries a few percent of the engine's propellant
One centre exhaust pipe
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant steel or nickel alloy tubing.

parts.name: Centre engine turbine exhaust

parts.description: Hydraulic ram that tilts the engine on its gimbal.

details.didYouKnow: In the final seconds before landing, the actuators are making constant tiny corrections, much like balancing a broom on your hand.
details.howItWorks: The centre engine's actuators tilt it on its gimbal, helping steer on the way up and doing most of the steering during the landing burn. They respond quickly to keep the booster upright and centred over the pad. Like the others, they use pressurised kerosene as hydraulic fluid.
keyNumbers: Tilts up to about 5 degrees
Corrects many times a second
Steers to a landing within a few metres
details.madeOf: Steel hydraulic cylinders and valves.

parts.name: Centre engine steering actuator

parts.description: Duct carrying kerosene from the tank to the turbopump.

details.didYouKnow: At landing, the booster has only a few percent of its fuel left, so getting every last drop into this line matters.
details.howItWorks: This line delivers kerosene to the centre engine's turbopump from the bottom of the fuel tank. Since the centre engine is used on landing, its feed line must keep supplying fuel even when the tank is nearly empty. Valves and baffles near the outlet help keep gas bubbles out.
keyNumbers: Carries about 90 kg of fuel per second
Roughly 10 to 15 cm in diameter
Supplies the engine used for landing
details.madeOf: Aluminium or stainless-steel tubing with flexible bellows to allow the engine to gimbal.

parts.name: Centre engine fuel feed line

summary: A 75 m reusable orbital launcher: nine-engine booster with landing legs and grid fins, a vacuum-engine upper stage, and a satellite inside a clamshell fairing.

name: Electric Car Drive Unit
overview:
A drive unit is what an electric car has where a petrol car has its engine and gearbox. It sits between the rear wheels and turns electricity from the battery into the torque that turns them.

It has three main parts. The inverter on top takes the battery's direct current and, by switching transistors thousands of times a second, turns it into three-phase alternating current. That current flows through copper windings in the motor's stator and makes a rotating magnetic field. The rotor, studded with permanent magnets, is dragged round by that field, up to about 18,000 rpm, with no contact and almost no wear.

That speed is far too high for the wheels, so a two-stage gearbox steps it down about nine to one. The differential then lets the left and right wheels turn at different speeds through corners. There's no clutch and no gear changing: one ratio covers everything from a standing start to top speed, and when you lift off, the motor works as a generator to recharge the battery.

parts.description: Cast-aluminium cover sealing the inverter electronics against water and dust.

details.didYouKnow: Inverter lids often carry a warning label because opening one can expose parts still charged by the capacitor; technicians wait for it to discharge before touching anything inside.
details.howItWorks: The lid bolts down onto the inverter housing over a rubber or formed-in-place gasket, so the delicate electronics stay dry even when the car drives through deep puddles or gets pressure-washed. Being metal, it also acts as part of a shielded box that keeps the fast-switching electrical noise inside from interfering with the car's radio and other electronics.
keyNumbers: Sealing typically meets IP67: dust-tight and survives immersion to about 1 m
Wall thickness roughly 2 to 4 mm
Usually held by around 10 to 20 small bolts
details.madeOf: Usually die-cast or pressed aluminium, which is light, easy to shape with stiffening ribs, and conducts well enough to work as an electromagnetic shield.

parts.name: Inverter lid

parts.description: Microcontroller and gate drivers that switch the transistors thousands of times a second to shape the motor current.

details.didYouKnow: Most of the clever behaviour of an electric motor, such as smooth launches and regenerative braking, lives in this board's software, which is why some cars gain power or efficiency through over-the-air updates.
details.howItWorks: A microcontroller reads the driver's accelerator request, the rotor angle from the resolver and current sensors on each phase, then calculates thousands of times a second exactly when each transistor should switch. Isolated gate-driver chips turn those low-voltage logic signals into the stronger pulses that flip the power modules on and off, while keeping the hundreds of volts on the power side safely separated from the logic side.
keyNumbers: Switching commands typically issued at about 10 to 20 kHz
Control loop runs roughly every 50 to 100 microseconds
Logic side runs at about 3.3 to 5 V, isolated from about 350 to 400 V
details.madeOf: A multilayer glass-fibre circuit board (FR-4) with soldered chips, often given a thin conformal coating to protect against moisture and vibration.

parts.name: Control board

parts.description: Silicon-carbide MOSFETs that turn the battery's DC into one of the three AC phases driving the motor.

details.didYouKnow: The Model 3 was widely reported as the first mass-market car to use silicon-carbide transistors in its main inverter, a move much of the industry later followed.
details.howItWorks: Each phase has a high-side and a low-side switch; turning them on and off in turn connects the U output alternately to the battery's plus and minus. By varying how long each switch stays on (pulse-width modulation), the inverter makes the average voltage rise and fall like a sine wave, and the motor's windings smooth those pulses into a near-sinusoidal current.
keyNumbers: Handles peak currents of very roughly 500 to 1,000 A
SiC chips can run at up to about 175 °C
Switch transitions take well under a microsecond
details.madeOf: Silicon-carbide chips soldered or sintered onto a copper-and-ceramic substrate, encased in plastic, with a copper base that presses onto the coolant-cooled floor of the housing.

parts.name: Power module, phase U

parts.description: Silicon-carbide MOSFETs that turn the battery's DC into one of the three AC phases driving the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Silicon carbide is so hard that it was first used as an abrasive called carborundum, long before anyone made transistors from it.
details.howItWorks: Phase V does the same job as U but runs 120 degrees later in the electrical cycle, so the three phases together create a magnetic field that rotates smoothly around the stator. The control board staggers its switching pattern, and the module sends its output down busbar V into the motor windings.
keyNumbers: Phases spaced 120 degrees apart electrically
Inverter efficiency typically about 98 to 99 percent
Blocking voltage rating typically about 650 V for a 400 V car
details.madeOf: Silicon carbide, a hard compound of silicon and carbon, is used instead of ordinary silicon because it blocks high voltage in a thinner layer and wastes less energy each time it switches.

parts.name: Power module, phase V

parts.description: Silicon-carbide MOSFETs that turn the battery's DC into one of the three AC phases driving the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Because SiC switches waste so little energy, a SiC inverter can add a few percent to a car's range compared with an older silicon-IGBT inverter, with the same battery.
details.howItWorks: The W module completes the set: at any instant the currents in U, V and W add up to zero, so current flowing out through one phase returns through the others. During regenerative braking the same switches run in reverse, rectifying the motor's generated AC back into DC to charge the battery.
keyNumbers: Losses per module typically only tens to a few hundred watts
Each SiC die is only a few millimetres across
Coolant beneath it is usually kept below about 65 °C
details.madeOf: Plastic-moulded package around SiC dies; the chips are bonded to the leads with aluminium or copper wires or ribbons, and the module is mounted with thermal paste or sintered silver to pass heat into the coolant plate.

parts.name: Power module, phase W

parts.description: Film capacitor that smooths the battery current feeding the power modules.

details.didYouKnow: Metallised film capacitors are self-healing: if a tiny spark punches through the film, the thin metal around the hole vaporises and isolates the fault, and the capacitor keeps working.
details.howItWorks: When the transistors switch, they demand sudden bursts of current far faster than the battery cable can deliver because of its inductance. The capacitor sits right beside the power modules and supplies those bursts locally, keeping the DC voltage steady and stopping ripple and voltage spikes from travelling back to the battery.
keyNumbers: Capacitance typically several hundred microfarads
Rated at roughly 450 to 500 V DC
Film only a few micrometres thick
details.madeOf: Rolled layers of thin polypropylene film coated with a metal film a few nanometres thick, potted in resin inside a plastic case; film is used because it handles high ripple current and heals itself after small breakdowns.

parts.name: DC-link capacitor

parts.description: Cast tray that holds the electronics; coolant flows through channels in its floor.

details.didYouKnow: Mounting the inverter directly on the motor, rather than in a separate box with cables, saves weight and cost and cuts electrical noise because the high-current paths are only centimetres long.
details.howItWorks: The housing is the inverter's backbone and its radiator: the power modules sit on its floor, and coolant from the car's thermal loop flows through channels or pin-fins just beneath them to pull away their heat. It also anchors the control board, capacitor and connectors, and bolts directly onto the motor so the phase busbars can be short.
keyNumbers: Coolant flow typically a few litres per minute through the plate
Must shed up to a few kilowatts of heat at full power
Aluminium conducts heat roughly 4 times better than steel
details.madeOf: High-pressure die-cast aluminium alloy, chosen because it is light, conducts heat well and can be cast with complex internal coolant passages in one piece.

parts.name: Inverter housing

parts.description: Orange-sheathed plug that brings ~350 V DC from the battery pack.

details.didYouKnow: Firefighters and mechanics are trained to treat any orange cable in an electric car as potentially lethal, which is why the colour is used so consistently across brands.
details.howItWorks: Two large pins carry the DC plus and minus from the battery, while a small extra loop of contacts called the high-voltage interlock tells the car whether the plug is fully seated. If the connector is pulled while live, the interlock opens first and the battery contactors switch off before the main pins can arc.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 350 to 400 V DC
Handles continuous currents of a few hundred amps
Interlock pins are typically a few millimetres shorter than the power pins
details.madeOf: Silver- or tin-plated copper contacts in a glass-filled plastic body, with a braided shield and orange insulation on the cable; orange is the industry's standard warning colour for high voltage.

parts.name: High-voltage connector

parts.description: Copper bar carrying one AC phase from the inverter down to the stator windings.

details.didYouKnow: In a three-phase system no return wire is needed: the current going out along U comes back along V and W, so three bars do the work that six would in separate circuits.
details.howItWorks: Busbar U links the U power module's output to the start of the U winding in the stator. A solid bar is used rather than a cable because it carries hundreds of amps with low resistance and low inductance, and it is often threaded through a current sensor so the control board can measure exactly what is flowing.
keyNumbers: Carries peak currents of very roughly 500 to 1,000 A
Cross-section typically tens of square millimetres
Copper resistivity about 0.017 micro-ohm metres
details.madeOf: Pure copper, often tin-plated at the joints, because copper has the highest conductivity of any affordable metal.

parts.name: Phase busbar U

parts.description: Copper bar carrying one AC phase from the inverter down to the stator windings.

details.didYouKnow: At high frequencies current crowds toward the outside of a conductor (the skin effect), which is one reason designers favour flat bars with lots of surface area.
details.howItWorks: Busbar V feeds the second phase. Its current alternates direction many times per second, with a frequency set by motor speed: the faster the rotor spins, the faster the inverter has to swing the current back and forth along this bar.
keyNumbers: AC frequency up to roughly 1,000 Hz or more at top speed
Joints usually bolted at around 5 to 10 N m
Often only a few centimetres long
details.madeOf: Electrolytic-grade copper strip, stamped and bent to shape, usually sleeved or coated in insulation wherever it passes close to the housing.

parts.name: Phase busbar V

parts.description: Copper bar carrying one AC phase from the inverter down to the stator windings.

details.didYouKnow: Copper for electrical use must be extremely pure, typically over 99.9 percent, because even tiny impurities noticeably increase its resistance.
details.howItWorks: Busbar W carries the third phase down into the motor. The three bars are usually laid out close and parallel so their magnetic fields largely cancel, which keeps stray inductance low and reduces voltage spikes when the transistors switch.
keyNumbers: Heats by only tens of degrees even at full power
Insulation rated well above the roughly 400 V working voltage
Three phases carry equal current, 120 degrees apart
details.madeOf: Copper bar, sometimes laminated together with the other phases and thin insulating sheets into a single sandwich to save space.

parts.name: Phase busbar W

parts.description: Bolted cap closing the far end of the motor; carries the rear bearing.

details.didYouKnow: If the bearing seat were even slightly off-centre, the rotor's magnets would pull harder on one side of the gap, causing noise and vibration.
details.howItWorks: The end cover closes the back of the motor housing and holds the rear bearing exactly on the motor axis, so the rotor stays centred inside the stator with only a small air gap. It often also houses the resolver and has oil passages that drain lubricant from the bearing back to the sump.
keyNumbers: Air gap it helps maintain is typically under 1 mm
Bearing bore machined to within about 0.01 to 0.02 mm
Held by 8 flange bolts in this unit
details.madeOf: Die-cast aluminium, machined precisely at the bearing seat, because it must be light yet hold the bearing within a few hundredths of a millimetre of true.

parts.name: Motor end cover

parts.description: One of eight flange bolts holding the end cover on.

details.didYouKnow: Aluminium expands about twice as much as steel when it heats up, so engineers have to make sure the bolts keep their clamping force as the motor warms and cools.
details.howItWorks: The bolts clamp the end cover to the motor housing, squeezing the seal between them so oil cannot leak out. They are tightened in a criss-cross pattern so the cover seats evenly and the bearing stays aligned.
keyNumbers: Typically about M6 to M8 in size
Tightened to roughly 10 to 25 N m
Usually property class 8.8 or 10.9 steel
details.madeOf: High-strength alloy steel, usually zinc-flake coated to resist corrosion, since it must stay tight through years of heat cycling against aluminium.

parts.name: End cover bolt

parts.description: Position sensor that tells the inverter exactly where the rotor is, so it can time each pulse of current.

details.didYouKnow: Resolvers were developed for aircraft and military equipment because they are so robust, and the same principle now runs in almost every electric car motor.
details.howItWorks: A resolver is a kind of rotary transformer: a coil on the stator side is fed a high-frequency signal, and a shaped steel rotor on the motor shaft changes how strongly that signal couples into two pickup coils set 90 degrees apart. Comparing the two outputs gives the rotor's angle, which the inverter needs to line up the magnetic field with the magnets.
keyNumbers: Excitation signal typically about 10 kHz
Angle accuracy usually a fraction of a degree
Works up to well beyond 18,000 rpm
details.madeOf: Laminated electrical steel and fine enamelled copper wire, with no electronics on the moving part, so it shrugs off heat, oil and vibration.

parts.name: Resolver

parts.description: Ball bearing supporting the rotor shaft at the end-cover side.

details.didYouKnow: Fast-switching inverters can induce small voltages on the motor shaft that spark across a bearing's oil film, leaving a washboard pattern called fluting, so EV bearings often need special protection.
details.howItWorks: This deep-groove ball bearing supports the rotor's far end, while a second bearing near the gearbox supports the other end. It keeps the rotor centred and lets it spin with very little friction, and it is lubricated by the same oil that cools the motor.
keyNumbers: Spins at up to about 18,000 rpm
Ball diameter typically several millimetres
Expected to last the life of the car, often over 300,000 km
details.madeOf: Hardened bearing steel rings and balls; some EV motors use ceramic balls or insulated outer rings to stop stray currents from the inverter pitting the races.

parts.name: Rear rotor bearing

parts.description: Laminated steel cylinder carrying the magnets; it spins up to about 18,000 rpm.

details.didYouKnow: At top speed the outside of the rotor moves faster than a Formula 1 car, so the thin steel bridges holding the magnets in must withstand enormous centrifugal force.
details.howItWorks: The rotor carries the magnets and is pulled round by the rotating magnetic field from the stator. It is built from hundreds of thin steel sheets stacked together so that eddy currents cannot circulate freely, and the slots punched into those sheets both hold the magnets and create the steel paths that produce extra reluctance torque.
keyNumbers: Spins up to about 18,000 rpm
Surface speed at top rpm roughly 500 km/h
Laminations typically about 0.25 to 0.35 mm thick
details.madeOf: Thin silicon-steel laminations stamped, stacked and bonded or welded together, with the magnets glued or held by resin inside their pockets.

parts.name: Rotor core

parts.description: Neodymium magnet buried in the rotor; the V-shaped pairs add reluctance torque to the magnets' pull.

details.didYouKnow: Neodymium magnets lose strength permanently if they get too hot, which is a big reason the motor is cooled so carefully with oil.
details.howItWorks: Each magnet's field locks on to the rotating field produced by the stator, pulling the rotor round. Because the magnets are buried in a V shape rather than glued to the surface, the steel around them also prefers to line up with the stator's field, adding a second source of torque called reluctance torque.
keyNumbers: 12 magnets in this model, in V-shaped pairs
Remanent field typically about 1.2 to 1.4 tesla
Usually rated to work up to roughly 150 to 180 °C
details.madeOf: Sintered neodymium-iron-boron, the strongest commercial permanent magnet, often with a little dysprosium or terbium added so it keeps its strength when hot, plus a nickel or epoxy coating against corrosion.

parts.name: Rotor magnet

parts.description: Hollow steel shaft running from the rotor into the gearbox, where it carries the input gear.

details.didYouKnow: A hollow shaft is almost as stiff in twisting as a solid one of the same outside size, because most of the strength comes from the metal near the outer surface.
details.howItWorks: The shaft runs through the centre of the rotor stack, carries its torque to the gearbox and turns on the two rotor bearings. It is hollow so that oil can be pumped down its middle and flung outward through holes to cool the rotor and magnets from the inside.
keyNumbers: Transmits roughly 300 to 450 N m of motor torque
Typically turns about 4,000 to 5,000 times per km driven
Bore usually around 10 to 20 mm across
details.madeOf: Alloy steel, machined and induction-hardened at the bearing journals and splines; making it hollow saves weight with little loss of stiffness.

parts.name: Rotor shaft

parts.description: Stack of thin electrical-steel laminations with slots that hold the copper windings.

details.didYouKnow: Adding silicon to iron raises its electrical resistance, which shrinks the wasteful eddy currents that would otherwise heat the core.
details.howItWorks: The stator is the stationary ring that surrounds the rotor. When current flows through the copper windings in its slots, the steel teeth channel and concentrate the resulting magnetic field across the narrow air gap to the rotor, and the three phases make that field spin.
keyNumbers: Silicon content typically about 3 percent
Usually around 48 to 72 slots in this class of motor
Stack length roughly 10 to 20 cm
details.madeOf: Hundreds of thin non-oriented silicon-steel laminations, each insulated with a thin coating and stacked into a solid core, to cut the eddy-current losses that a solid block would suffer.
