parts.name: Stator core

parts.description: Bent copper hairpins — flat bars welded end to end — forming the three-phase winding.

details.didYouKnow: Hairpin stators are well suited to robots, which is one reason they spread quickly through high-volume EV factories.
details.howItWorks: Instead of winding round wire, U-shaped flat copper bars called hairpins are pushed into the stator slots from one side. Their closed bends form this end of the winding, and the bars pack tightly in the slots, so more copper fits into the same space and the motor makes more torque with less heating.
keyNumbers: Slot fill typically about 70 percent versus about 45 percent for round wire
Bar cross-section roughly a few millimetres by a few millimetres
Enamel insulation only about 0.1 to 0.2 mm thick
details.madeOf: Rectangular enamel-insulated copper bar, bent into shape by machines; the flat profile packs far more tightly than round wire.

parts.name: Hairpin winding end (gearbox side)

parts.description: Welded ends of the hairpin conductors on the other side of the stator.

details.didYouKnow: The exposed end turns are an ideal spot for cooling, so many drive units drip or spray oil straight onto them.
details.howItWorks: On this side the open legs of the hairpins stick out of the stator and are twisted so that each one lines up with a leg from another hairpin. The pairs are then welded together, joining all the separate bars into continuous coils for the three phases.
keyNumbers: A stator typically has a few hundred welds
Each laser weld takes a fraction of a second
Oil sprayed on these end turns removes much of the winding's heat
details.madeOf: The same enamelled copper bar, with the insulation stripped at the tips so they can be laser-welded, then usually coated with resin or varnish to insulate and strengthen the joints.

parts.name: Hairpin winding end (cover side)

parts.description: Cast-aluminium sleeve around the stator; oil sprayed inside it carries the motor's heat away.

details.didYouKnow: Electric motors are often well over 90 percent efficient, but at full power even a few percent loss means several kilowatts of heat that this housing and its oil must carry away.
details.howItWorks: The housing grips the stator firmly so it cannot twist under the reaction torque, and holds the front bearing in line with the end cover. Oil from the pump is sprayed or dripped on the stator and windings inside it, collects in a sump and returns to the heat exchanger.
keyNumbers: Must resist reaction torque of up to about 450 N m
Oil inside typically runs at about 60 to 90 °C
Shrink-fitting heats it to roughly 200 °C during assembly
details.madeOf: High-pressure die-cast aluminium alloy; the stator is often shrink-fitted in by heating the housing so it expands, inserting the stator, and letting it cool to a tight grip.

parts.name: Motor housing

parts.description: Outer half of the gearbox case, sealing in the oil that lubricates the gears and cools the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Without engine noise to mask it, gear whine is one of the loudest sounds in an EV, so engineers shape gearbox casings carefully to keep them quiet.
details.howItWorks: The cover closes the outer side of the gearbox, holding the far bearings of the gear shafts and sealing in the oil. As the gears spin they splash oil up onto its inside walls, from where it trickles back down to lubricate bearings and teeth.
keyNumbers: Gearbox oil fill typically a couple of litres
Oil is low-viscosity, similar to automatic transmission fluid
Sealing face kept flat to within a few hundredths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Die-cast aluminium with stiffening ribs, which keep it light and help stop it vibrating like a loudspeaker and radiating gear whine.

parts.name: Gearbox cover

parts.description: Inner half of the gearbox case, bolted to the motor housing; it holds the shaft bearings.

details.didYouKnow: Many drive units combine the motor and gearbox housings into shared castings, which cuts parts and joints compared with bolting a separate motor to a separate transmission.
details.howItWorks: The case is the structural heart of the gearbox, bolted to the motor housing and holding the bearings for all three shafts exactly parallel at the right spacing. Accurate bearing positions matter because even small misalignment makes gear teeth wear unevenly and whine.
keyNumbers: Holds 3 parallel shafts: motor, intermediate and differential
Shaft centre distances held to within about 0.02 to 0.05 mm
Resists reaction torque of a few thousand N m at the output
details.madeOf: High-pressure die-cast aluminium, precision-machined at the bearing bores, combining low weight with enough stiffness to keep the gears in mesh under full torque.

parts.name: Gearbox case

parts.description: Small gear on the motor shaft — the first of two reduction stages (about 9:1 overall).

details.didYouKnow: EV gears use helical, slanted teeth so that several teeth are in contact at once, which spreads the load and makes them much quieter than straight-cut gears.
details.howItWorks: The pinion sits on the end of the rotor shaft and turns at full motor speed. It has few teeth, so each turn of the large intermediate gear it drives takes several turns of the pinion, cutting speed and multiplying torque by the same factor.
keyNumbers: Spins up to about 18,000 rpm
Typically has roughly 15 to 25 teeth
Tooth surface hardness around 58 to 62 HRC
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel: the tooth surfaces are carburised to be very hard and wear-resistant while the core stays tough, then the teeth are precision ground for quiet running.

parts.name: Input pinion

parts.description: Large gear driven by the input pinion; it slows the motor speed about threefold.

details.didYouKnow: Gear teeth are given tiny deliberate shape corrections, called micro-geometry, measured in micrometres, to cancel out bending under load and keep the mesh quiet.
details.howItWorks: This large gear meshes with the input pinion and forms the first reduction stage, turning about a third as fast as the motor. It is fixed to the intermediate shaft, so its torque passes straight to the intermediate pinion beside it.
keyNumbers: First-stage reduction roughly 3:1
Turns at up to about 6,000 rpm
Gear tooth contact efficiency typically about 98 to 99 percent per stage
details.madeOf: Forged, machined and case-hardened alloy steel, with the teeth ground after heat treatment to correct any distortion.

parts.name: Intermediate gear

parts.description: Second-stage pinion sharing the intermediate shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Splitting the reduction into two stages keeps every gear a sensible size; doing 9:1 in one step would need a huge output gear or a tiny, overloaded pinion.
details.howItWorks: The intermediate pinion shares the shaft with the intermediate gear, so it turns at the same speed but, being smaller, pushes harder on the final-drive gear it meshes with. This starts the second reduction stage, where the teeth carry far more force than in the first.
keyNumbers: Second-stage reduction roughly 3:1
Carries roughly 3 times the motor's torque
Typically about 15 to 25 teeth
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel, usually cut as part of the shaft or pressed on with splines, and made wider than the first-stage gears to cope with the higher torque.

parts.name: Intermediate pinion

parts.description: Shaft carrying the intermediate gear and pinion between their two bearings.

details.didYouKnow: Helical gears push sideways along their shafts as well as round them, so the bearings must resist end-thrust as well as radial load.
details.howItWorks: The intermediate shaft links the two reduction stages, turning the speed-reduced output of the first stage into the input of the second. It spins on two bearings in the gearbox case and cover, and has to stay stiff so its two gears stay correctly meshed.
keyNumbers: Spins at up to about 6,000 rpm
Carries roughly 3 times motor torque
Supported by 2 bearings
details.madeOf: Alloy steel, machined and hardened, with ground bearing journals; tapered roller or ball bearings carry the side forces created by the helical teeth.

parts.name: Intermediate shaft

parts.description: Large gear bolted to the differential; the second reduction stage.

details.didYouKnow: Because an electric motor works across such a wide speed range, this single fixed ratio replaces the whole set of gears a petrol car needs.
details.howItWorks: The final-drive gear is the biggest in the gearbox and is bolted to the differential case. Driven by the intermediate pinion, it completes the overall reduction of about 9:1, so the differential and wheels turn at about one ninth of motor speed with roughly nine times the torque.
keyNumbers: Overall ratio about 9:1
Turns at up to about 2,000 rpm
Output torque can reach very roughly 3,000 to 4,000 N m
details.madeOf: Large case-hardened alloy steel gear, ground for quiet running and bolted or welded to the differential case.

parts.name: Final-drive gear

parts.description: Housing for the differential gears, which let the two rear wheels turn at different speeds in corners.

details.didYouKnow: An open differential sends equal torque to both wheels, so if one wheel is on ice, both get only the little torque the slipping wheel can use; EVs fix this by braking the spinning wheel with traction control.
details.howItWorks: The differential case spins with the final-drive gear and carries a cross pin holding the spider gears. When the car goes straight, everything turns together as one block; in a corner, the spider gears rotate on their pin so the outer wheel can go faster than the inner one while both still get equal torque.
keyNumbers: Carries the full output torque of a few thousand N m
In a tight turn, wheel speeds can differ by about 20 percent or more
Turns at up to about 2,000 rpm
details.madeOf: Usually cast ductile iron or forged steel, both strong and tough enough to carry the full output torque and resist shock loads.

parts.name: Differential case

parts.description: Bevel gear splined to the left axle shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The speeds of the two side gears always average to the speed of the differential case, so if one wheel stops completely, the other spins at twice the case speed.
details.howItWorks: The left side gear meshes with both spider gears and is splined to the left axle. When both wheels turn at the same speed it simply rotates with the case; when the left wheel slows in a left-hand corner, the spider gears roll around it and speed up the right side instead.
keyNumbers: Typically about 14 to 18 teeth
Carries half the output torque, roughly 1,500 to 2,000 N m
Usually backed by a thrust washer a millimetre or two thick
details.madeOf: Forged and case-hardened alloy steel bevel gear, with internal splines broached into its hub to grip the axle.

parts.name: Side gear (left)

parts.description: Bevel gear splined to the right axle shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The idea of the differential is old: one appeared in a steam carriage in France in the 1820s, long before the motor car.
details.howItWorks: The right side gear is the mirror of the left, splined to the right axle. In a right-hand bend the right wheel follows the tighter inner path, so this gear turns more slowly than the case while the left gear turns correspondingly faster.
keyNumbers: Splined hub typically has around 20 to 30 splines
Speed differences in normal corners usually under about 10 percent
Lubricated by splash from the gearbox oil
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel; bevel teeth are often precision forged nearly to final shape, which saves machining and leaves a strong grain flow in the teeth.

parts.name: Side gear (right)

parts.description: Small bevel gear that rolls between the side gears when the wheels turn at different speeds.

details.didYouKnow: On a straight road the spider gears barely move at all, which is why they can run for hundreds of thousands of kilometres on little more than a splash of oil.
details.howItWorks: The spider gear turns on the cross pin inside the differential case and meshes with both side gears at once. Going straight it does not spin on its pin and just carries the side gears round; in a corner it rotates, letting one side gear speed up as the other slows by the same amount.
keyNumbers: Typically about 9 to 11 teeth
Usually stationary on its pin when driving straight
Bevel teeth meet the side gears at 90 degrees
details.madeOf: Small case-hardened steel bevel gear with a smooth hardened bore that runs directly on the steel cross pin, lubricated by gearbox oil.

parts.name: Spider gear

parts.description: Second spider gear, opposite the first on the cross pin.

details.didYouKnow: If one wheel of a jacked-up car is turned by hand with the other held still, the spider gears spin, and the free wheel turns the opposite way.
details.howItWorks: The second spider gear sits opposite the first on the same cross pin. Having two shares the driving force between two sets of teeth and balances the forces on the side gears, so they are not pushed off-centre.
keyNumbers: 2 spider gears in this differential; heavy-duty ones may have 4
Each shares roughly half the load between the side gears
Spins only as fast as the wheel-speed difference requires
details.madeOf: Identical case-hardened steel to its partner, with a curved spherical back face that sits against a matching thrust washer in the case.

parts.name: Spider gear

parts.description: Hinged latch that locks into a toothed wheel when the car is put in Park.

details.didYouKnow: Because the pawl locks the gearbox rather than the wheels directly, an open differential means a car lifted on one side can still roll; that is why the handbrake is used too.
details.howItWorks: When the driver selects Park, a small actuator pushes this hinged pawl into the teeth of a parking wheel on one of the gearbox shafts, locking the gears and therefore the wheels. Its tooth is shaped so that if the car is still rolling faster than a walking pace it ratchets off rather than engaging and breaking.
keyNumbers: Usually engages only below about 3 to 5 km/h
Locks against a wheel with typically around 10 to 20 notches
Must hold the car on steep gradients of 20 percent or more
details.madeOf: Hardened steel, needed so the narrow tooth can hold the whole car on a slope without bending or wearing.

parts.name: Parking pawl

parts.description: Output shaft to the left wheel; it runs alongside the motor.

details.didYouKnow: A long, slim shaft acts like a torsion spring, twisting slightly under load, which can actually help smooth out sudden jolts of torque.
details.howItWorks: The left axle stub is splined into the left side gear and carries its torque out of the gearbox. Because the gearbox sits off to one side, this shaft runs alongside the motor to reach the far side of the unit, passing through a seal that keeps the oil in.
keyNumbers: Carries up to roughly 1,500 to 2,000 N m
Spins at up to about 2,000 rpm
Typically about 25 to 35 mm diameter
details.madeOf: Induction-hardened medium-carbon alloy steel, which gives a hard, fatigue-resistant surface on the splines while the core stays tough enough to twist slightly without breaking.

parts.name: Left axle stub

parts.description: Short output shaft to the right wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Unequal-length shafts can make a car tug sideways under hard acceleration, called torque steer, but with rear-wheel drive this has very little effect on steering.
details.howItWorks: The right stub is much shorter because the differential sits on the right side of the unit. It takes torque from the right side gear and passes it through a lip seal to the right output flange.
keyNumbers: Often only around 10 to 20 cm long
Turns about 470 times per kilometre with a typical tyre
Seal lip runs on a surface polished to a fine finish
details.madeOf: Forged and machined alloy steel, splined at both ends and hardened where seals and bearings run.

parts.name: Right axle stub

parts.description: Joint where the left half-shaft to the wheel plugs in.

details.didYouKnow: A plain universal joint makes the output shaft speed up and slow down twice per turn when it is bent; a constant-velocity joint cancels this so the wheel turns smoothly.
details.howItWorks: This flange is where the left half-shaft connects. The half-shaft has constant-velocity joints at each end, so the wheel can move up and down on the suspension and the drive keeps turning smoothly without its speed pulsing.
keyNumbers: Allows joint angles of roughly 20 degrees or more
Passes up to roughly 2,000 N m to the wheel
CV joints often have 6 steel balls
details.madeOf: Forged steel, splined to the axle stub and machined where the joint or boot attaches.

parts.name: Left output flange

parts.description: Joint where the right half-shaft to the wheel plugs in.

details.didYouKnow: A torn CV boot is one of the most common drivetrain faults; once dirt gets into the grease, the joint wears out quickly.
details.howItWorks: The right output flange connects the right half-shaft, which runs out to the right rear hub. Its inner joint can usually slide in and out a little to allow for the change in shaft length as the suspension moves.
keyNumbers: Plunge travel typically a few centimetres
Spins at up to about 2,000 rpm
Boot holds roughly 100 g or more of grease
details.madeOf: Forged and hardened steel; the joint itself is packed with grease and protected by a flexible rubber or plastic boot.

parts.name: Right output flange

parts.description: Cast bracket bolting the drive unit to the car's rear subframe.

details.didYouKnow: When you accelerate hard, the whole drive unit tries to rotate the opposite way to the wheels, so its mounts work hardest during launches and regenerative braking.
details.howItWorks: The bracket bolts the drive unit to the car's rear subframe, carrying its weight and resisting its tendency to twist when it delivers torque to the wheels. It works together with rubber bushings so the unit is held firmly but not rigidly.
keyNumbers: Supports a drive unit weighing roughly 80 to 100 kg
Resists reaction torque of a few thousand N m
Usually held by bolts of about M10 to M12
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium, shaped with ribs for stiffness at low weight; casting allows complex shapes that put metal only where loads flow.

parts.name: Mounting bracket

parts.description: Rubber bushing that stops motor whine and vibration reaching the cabin.

details.didYouKnow: EV cabins are so quiet that motor whine at a few kilohertz becomes noticeable, so drive-unit mounts are tuned more carefully than engine mounts once were.
details.howItWorks: The bushing is a rubber cushion between the bracket and the subframe. It is stiff enough to stop the unit moving much under torque, but soft enough to absorb the high-pitched whine and vibration from the motor and gears before they reach the body.
keyNumbers: Rubber hardness typically about 50 to 70 Shore A
Allows movement of only a few millimetres
Targets noise from a few hundred to a few thousand hertz
details.madeOf: Natural or synthetic rubber bonded to steel or aluminium sleeves; rubber is chosen because it absorbs vibration energy rather than passing it on.

parts.name: Rubber mount bushing

parts.description: Electric pump that circulates gearbox oil over the gears and through the motor to cool it.

details.didYouKnow: Some drive units can deliberately run the motor inefficiently to make extra heat, which the oil and coolant loop then use to warm the battery in cold weather.
details.howItWorks: The pump draws oil from the gearbox sump, pushes it through the filter and heat exchanger, and delivers it to jets and passages that spray the stator windings, flow down the hollow rotor shaft, and lubricate the bearings and gears. Being electric, it can run at any speed the control system chooses, even when the car is stopped.
keyNumbers: Typically flows a few litres per minute
Pressure usually only about 1 to 3 bar
Draws power on the order of tens of watts
details.madeOf: A small brushless electric motor driving a gerotor or gear pump, in a plastic or aluminium body sealed against the oil.

parts.name: Oil pump

parts.description: Screw-in filter that catches wear particles from the gears.

details.didYouKnow: Most of the metal particles in a new gearbox come from the first few hundred kilometres, as the gear teeth bed in against each other.
details.howItWorks: All the oil from the pump passes through the filter, which traps tiny metal particles worn from gear teeth and bearings, as well as any debris left from manufacturing. Clean oil keeps the bearings and gear surfaces from being scratched and stops particles reaching the motor windings.
keyNumbers: Filters particles down to roughly 20 to 40 micrometres
Service intervals can be very long, often over 100,000 km
Contains a bypass valve that opens if the element clogs
details.madeOf: A pleated paper or synthetic-fibre element inside a painted steel canister, often with a magnet nearby to grab steel particles.

parts.name: Oil filter

parts.description: Stack of thin plates where hot motor oil gives its heat to the car's coolant loop.

details.didYouKnow: Oil cools the motor well because it does not conduct electricity and can touch the windings directly, but water-glycol carries heat away much better, so EVs use both.
details.howItWorks: Hot oil from the motor and gears flows through alternate layers of this plate stack, while water-glycol coolant from the car flows through the layers in between. Heat passes through the thin metal walls from oil to coolant, and the coolant carries it to the radiator or to wherever the car needs heat.
keyNumbers: Plates typically well under 1 mm thick
Can move a few kilowatts of heat
Usually has tens of plates
details.madeOf: Thin aluminium plates brazed together in a furnace into one leak-tight block, because aluminium is light and conducts heat very well.

parts.name: Oil-to-coolant heat exchanger

parts.description: Brings coolant from the radiator loop into the heat exchanger and inverter.

details.didYouKnow: Many EVs route the same coolant through the battery, cabin heater and drive unit, using valves to share heat between them.
details.howItWorks: This hose brings cooled water-glycol from the car's thermal system into the drive unit. It typically passes first under the inverter's power modules, which are most sensitive to heat, and then on to the oil heat exchanger.
keyNumbers: Coolant is typically about 50 percent water, 50 percent glycol
Flow usually around 10 to 20 litres per minute
Inlet temperature normally below about 65 °C
details.madeOf: Reinforced EPDM rubber, which resists heat, glycol and ageing while staying flexible enough to absorb vibration between the drive unit and car body.

parts.name: Coolant inlet hose

parts.description: Returns warmed coolant to the car's thermal system.

details.didYouKnow: Glycol in the coolant lowers its freezing point to well below minus 30 °C and also raises its boiling point.
details.howItWorks: The outlet hose carries coolant away after it has collected heat from the inverter and the motor oil. That warm coolant either goes to the radiator to dump heat, or, in cold weather, to the battery or cabin, so the drive unit's waste heat is not entirely wasted.
keyNumbers: Coolant leaves typically a few to about 10 °C warmer than it entered
Hose bore usually around 16 to 25 mm
Rated for system pressures up to about 2 bar
details.madeOf: Reinforced EPDM rubber hose with quick-connect fittings, which allow fast assembly on the factory line.

parts.name: Coolant outlet hose

summary: The motor, inverter and gearbox that replace the engine in an electric car, modelled on the rear drive unit in cars like the Tesla Model 3: a permanent-magnet motor spinning up to 18,000 rpm, a silicon-carbide inverter, and a 9:1 two-stage gearbox with differential.

name: Camera Drone
overview:
A camera drone is a small flying robot built to hold a camera perfectly steady in the air. It's a quadcopter: four propellers, each on its own electric motor, provide all the lift and all the steering. There are no control surfaces; it moves by spinning some propellers faster than others.

Two propellers spin clockwise and two anticlockwise so their twisting forces cancel. To move forward, the drone speeds up its rear motors and tilts; to turn, it speeds up one diagonal pair. The flight computer makes these adjustments hundreds of times a second, using gyroscopes, accelerometers, GPS, a compass and downward cameras, so it can hover in one spot by itself.

The camera hangs under the nose on a three-axis gimbal: small motors that counter every tilt and shake of the body, so the footage stays level and smooth. A smart battery powers everything for around half an hour, and the arms fold in so the whole thing packs down to about the size of a water bottle.

parts.description: Moulded plastic cover over the nose electronics.

details.didYouKnow: Many folding drones are designed to weigh under 250 g, a threshold below which several countries relax registration rules, so every gram of shell plastic is fought over.
details.howItWorks: The upper shell is a thin aerodynamic skin rather than a structural part: it clips or screws onto the chassis and keeps rain spray, dust and fingers away from the circuit boards. Its smooth, rounded shape cuts drag in fast forward flight, and it leaves an opening at the back where the battery slides in to complete the body's outline.
keyNumbers: Wall thickness typically about 1 mm
Weighs roughly 15 to 30 g
Whole drone usually under about 900 g
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded polycarbonate or a polycarbonate blend, which is light, tough enough to survive a knock and easy to mould with clips and screw bosses built in.

parts.name: Upper shell

parts.description: Underside of the body, with windows for the downward sensors and vents for cooling air.

details.didYouKnow: The sensor windows are often given an anti-reflective coating, because a scratch or glare on them can confuse the vision system enough to make the drone drift.
details.howItWorks: The lower shell closes the body from underneath and carries the clear windows that the downward cameras and infrared height sensor look through. Slots near the front let the cooling fan draw in or exhaust air, and the gimbal hangs just ahead of it, so its shape is a compromise between airflow, sensor view and stiffness.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 to 4 sensor windows
Wall thickness about 1 mm
Ground clearance under the body roughly 3 to 5 cm
details.madeOf: Moulded polycarbonate or ABS blend, often with clear polycarbonate or glass sensor windows bonded in, chosen for low weight and impact resistance.

parts.name: Lower shell

parts.description: Rigid alloy spine that everything bolts to; it also spreads heat from the processors.

details.didYouKnow: Magnesium is the same metal used in some laptop frames and camera bodies, and in thin cast form it is surprisingly hard to set alight despite its reputation.
details.howItWorks: The chassis is the drone's backbone: the arm hinges, circuit boards, gimbal mount and battery rails all fix to it, so loads from the four motors pass through it rather than the plastic shells. Because it is metal and touches the hottest chips through thermal pads, it also acts as a large heat spreader, moving warmth towards the heat sink and the airflow.
keyNumbers: Magnesium is about a third lighter than aluminium
Density roughly 1.8 g per cubic cm
Chassis typically weighs about 30 to 60 g
details.madeOf: Usually a die-cast or machined magnesium alloy, the lightest structural metal in common use, which gives high stiffness for its weight and conducts heat well.

parts.name: Magnesium chassis

parts.description: Hollow arm carrying a motor at its tip; it swings in against the body for packing.

details.didYouKnow: If an arm flexes even slightly, the motor's thrust tilts with it, so arm stiffness directly affects how precisely the drone can hover.
details.howItWorks: Each arm holds a motor well out from the body so the four propellers do not overlap, and its length sets the leverage the flight controller has for tilting the drone. The front arms usually swing sideways and the rear arms swing down and under, letting the whole craft fold to roughly the size of a water bottle. The hollow inside carries the motor wires and often the antenna feed.
keyNumbers: Motor-to-motor diagonal typically about 30 to 40 cm
Each arm weighs roughly 10 to 20 g
Folds through about 90 to 180 degrees
details.madeOf: Glass- or carbon-fibre-reinforced nylon or polycarbonate, which is stiff enough to stop the motors wobbling yet slightly flexible so it can survive a crash.

parts.name: Folding arm

parts.description: Steel pivot with a detent that clicks the arm open or folded.

details.didYouKnow: Most folding drones refuse to take off, or warn the pilot, if an arm is not fully opened, because a half-locked arm can fold in flight.
details.howItWorks: The hinge pin is the axle each arm pivots on. A small spring-loaded detent or cam presses against notches so the arm clicks firmly into its open and folded positions, and the open position must be rigid enough that the arm does not creep under full motor thrust.
keyNumbers: Pin diameter typically about 2 to 4 mm
Rated for thousands of fold cycles
Detent holds against several newtons of thrust
details.madeOf: Hardened or stainless steel, because the pin is tiny yet takes repeated bending loads and must not wear loose over thousands of folds.

parts.name: Arm hinge pin

parts.description: Short foot under each motor that keeps the camera clear of the ground.

details.didYouKnow: On many folding drones the feet double as antenna housings, which keeps the antennas below the carbon and metal of the body where they would otherwise be shadowed.
details.howItWorks: The landing feet are the only parts that touch the ground on a normal landing, lifting the body high enough that the gimbal and lens never scrape. Their soft tips cushion the touchdown and grip smooth surfaces so the drone does not slide while the motors spin down.
keyNumbers: Typically 4 feet, one under each motor
Raise the body by roughly 2 to 4 cm
Each weighs only a few grams
details.madeOf: A rubber or thermoplastic elastomer tip over a moulded plastic stem, giving grip and shock absorption without adding much weight.

parts.name: Landing foot

parts.description: Antenna strip hidden in the landing foot; it carries the control link and live video.

details.didYouKnow: At 2.4 GHz a quarter of a wavelength is about 3 cm, which is why the antenna fits neatly inside a short landing foot.
details.howItWorks: These antennas send and receive the radio link to the remote controller, carrying stick commands up and compressed live video and telemetry down. Using several antennas spread around the craft lets the radio pick the strongest signal and combine paths, so the link survives as the drone turns and banks.
keyNumbers: Works on the 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz bands
Typical range up to about 10 to 15 km in open, unobstructed areas
Live video around 1080p at roughly 30 to 60 frames per second
details.madeOf: A thin copper trace on a flexible printed circuit or a small copper strip, since copper conducts well and can be shaped to fit inside the foot.

parts.name: Radio antenna

parts.description: LED that shows which way the drone is facing and blinks warnings.

details.didYouKnow: Some drones let you switch the front lights off during filming, because their glow can reflect into the shot when flying at night.
details.howItWorks: The arm lights tell the pilot which way the drone is pointing from a distance: by convention the front lights show one colour and the rear lights another. They also flash in coded patterns to signal GPS lock, low battery, sensor errors or calibration modes.
keyNumbers: Draws only about 20 milliamps or less
Visible from roughly a few hundred metres at dusk
Typically 4 lights, one per arm
details.madeOf: A small surface-mount LED chip behind a clear or diffusing plastic lens, chosen because LEDs are bright, efficient and almost weightless.

parts.name: Arm status light

parts.description: Hinged carbon-filled blade; it folds back for storage and swings out when the motor spins up.

details.didYouKnow: The blade is twisted along its length because the tip moves several times faster than the root, so it needs a shallower angle to keep the whole blade working evenly.
details.howItWorks: Each blade is a small rotating wing: its curved, twisted profile pushes air downward, and the reaction pushes the drone up. Because it is mounted on a pivot, centrifugal force swings it straight out the moment the motor spins up, and it folds back against the arm when the drone is packed.
keyNumbers: Diameter typically about 20 to 24 cm (8 to 9.5 inches)
Spins at up to roughly 8,000 to 10,000 rpm
Each blade weighs only about 3 to 5 g
details.madeOf: Glass- or carbon-fibre-filled nylon moulding, which is stiff enough to hold its aerofoil shape at high speed yet tough and cheap to replace after a strike.

parts.name: Propeller blade (leading)

parts.description: The second blade of each propeller, opposite the first.

details.didYouKnow: Propellers are often marked with a coloured ring or symbol so you fit the clockwise and anticlockwise ones to the right motors; swapping them means the drone flips on take-off.
details.howItWorks: The trailing blade sits exactly opposite the leading one so the propeller stays balanced; any mismatch in weight would shake the whole drone and blur the video. Two of the four propellers spin clockwise and two anticlockwise, so their twisting forces cancel, and each blade is shaped for its direction of spin.
keyNumbers: Blade tips reach roughly 100 m/s at full speed
Two-blade props are typical for this class
Balanced to within a fraction of a gram
details.madeOf: The same fibre-filled nylon as its partner, moulded as a matched pair so both blades share weight and shape closely.

parts.name: Propeller blade (trailing)

parts.description: Quick-release hub: push and twist to lock a propeller onto its motor.

details.didYouKnow: Folding props on a quick-release hub mean you can swap all four in under a minute in the field, with no tools at all.
details.howItWorks: The hub joins both blades to the motor and carries their pivots. A spring-loaded quick-release fitting lets you push it onto the motor and twist to lock, and the locking direction is chosen so the motor's own spin tightens it rather than loosening it.
keyNumbers: Fits or releases in about 1 to 2 seconds
Each blade pulls outward with tens of newtons at full speed
Hub weighs roughly 1 to 3 g
details.madeOf: Moulded reinforced nylon, sometimes with a small metal insert or spring, combining low weight with enough strength to resist the large centrifugal pull of the blades.

parts.name: Propeller hub

parts.description: Spinning outer can of the brushless motor, lined with permanent magnets.

details.didYouKnow: Outrunner motors produce lots of torque at low speed, which is why drones can drive propellers directly without any gearbox.
details.howItWorks: The bell is the part of the motor that actually spins: it is an outrunner design, with a ring of permanent magnets glued inside the can that turns around the fixed stator. As the stator's magnetic field rotates, it drags the magnets and so the bell round, and the propeller hub sits directly on top.
keyNumbers: Typically 12 to 14 magnet poles
Bell diameter roughly 2 to 3 cm
Spins at up to about 10,000 rpm
details.madeOf: A steel or aluminium can lined with strong neodymium magnets; steel helps carry the magnetic field around the back of the magnets so less of it is wasted.

parts.name: Motor bell

parts.description: Copper windings on a laminated core; the speed controller energises them in sequence to turn the bell.

details.didYouKnow: Drone motors are named by their stator size, so a '2008' motor has a stator about 20 mm across and 8 mm tall.
details.howItWorks: The stator stays still: it is a star of thin iron laminations with copper wire wound round each tooth. The speed controller switches current through the windings in a rotating sequence, building a magnetic field that steps round the stator and pulls the bell's magnets after it.
keyNumbers: Typically 9 or 12 wound teeth
Lamination sheets about 0.2 mm thick
Motor efficiency often around 80 to 90 percent
details.madeOf: Enamelled copper wire on a core of thin, insulated silicon-steel sheets; stacking thin sheets rather than using solid iron stops wasteful eddy currents that would heat the motor.

parts.name: Motor stator

parts.description: Base that bolts the motor to the arm and holds its bearings.

details.didYouKnow: Worn motor bearings are a common cause of a drone suddenly sounding gritty, and the extra vibration can show up as jelly-like ripples in the video.
details.howItWorks: The mount screws onto the end of the arm and carries the stator and the bearings that the bell's shaft spins in. It transfers the full thrust of the propeller into the arm, and holds the motor precisely square so the thrust points straight down.
keyNumbers: Usually 2 small ball bearings per motor
Held by about 3 to 4 tiny screws
Each motor produces up to roughly 500 to 1,000 g of thrust
details.madeOf: Machined or cast aluminium alloy, chosen for stiffness, light weight and its ability to conduct heat away from the stator.

parts.name: Motor mount

parts.description: Three-phase leads running through the arm from the speed controller to the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Swapping any two of a brushless motor's three wires reverses its direction of spin, a trick builders use to set clockwise and anticlockwise motors.
details.howItWorks: Three thin wires carry power from the speed controller to the three sets of windings in each motor. They run inside the hollow arm and must bend through the hinge each time the arm folds, so they are routed with a little slack to avoid fatigue.
keyNumbers: 3 wires per motor, 12 in total
Each carries a few amps in hover, roughly 10 A or more at full power
Typically about 24 to 28 AWG gauge
details.madeOf: Fine stranded copper with flexible silicone or PVC insulation; many fine strands survive repeated bending far better than one solid core.

parts.name: Motor wires

parts.description: Electronic speed controller: switches battery power into the motor's three phases thousands of times a second.

details.didYouKnow: Many speed controllers sense the motor's position from the voltage its spinning magnets generate in the unpowered winding, so no separate position sensor is needed.
details.howItWorks: The speed controller takes commands from the flight controller and turns steady battery current into the rotating three-phase pulses the motor needs. It uses tiny MOSFET transistors switched on and off tens of thousands of times a second, and changes the pulse width to vary motor speed almost instantly.
keyNumbers: Switches at roughly 16,000 to 48,000 times a second
Updates motor speed hundreds of times a second
Efficiency typically above about 90 percent
details.madeOf: A small circuit board with power MOSFETs, a microcontroller and copper heat-spreading planes, usually built onto or beside the main board in folding drones.

parts.name: Speed controller

parts.description: Slide-in pack that forms the rear top of the body; a button and four LEDs show charge.

details.didYouKnow: Because the battery is often the heaviest single part, its position is carefully chosen so the drone's centre of gravity sits right between the four motors.
details.howItWorks: The battery case holds the cells and management board as one sealed 'smart battery' that slides in and latches into the body, forming part of its shape. Pressing the button lights the LEDs to show charge in steps of about a quarter, and its gold-plated contacts carry both power and data to the drone.
keyNumbers: Pack typically about 3,500 to 5,000 mAh
Weighs roughly 250 to 350 g, a large share of the drone
Energy about 40 to 80 Wh
details.madeOf: Moulded polycarbonate or a flame-retardant plastic blend, which is light, tough and adds a layer of protection if a cell fails.

parts.name: Battery case

parts.description: One of three pouch cells in series, about 11.4 V together and good for roughly half an hour of flight.

details.didYouKnow: A pouch cell can swell like a pillow if it is damaged or stored fully charged for long, which is why smart batteries slowly discharge themselves to storage level.
details.howItWorks: Inside the pouch, thin sheets of anode and cathode are stacked with a separator soaked in a gel electrolyte; lithium ions shuttle from one side to the other as it charges and discharges. This cell sits at the bottom of the series stack, so its negative terminal is the pack's main negative connection.
keyNumbers: About 3.8 V nominal per cell
Full charge typically about 4.35 to 4.4 V
Can deliver roughly 5 to 10 times its capacity in amps
details.madeOf: A graphite anode and lithium cobalt or similar oxide cathode, sealed in a flexible aluminium-laminated pouch that is lighter than a metal can.

parts.name: Lithium-polymer cell 1

parts.description: One of three pouch cells in series, about 11.4 V together and good for roughly half an hour of flight.

details.didYouKnow: Lithium-polymer cells lose noticeable power in the cold, so pilots warm batteries in a pocket before winter flights, and some packs have built-in heaters.
details.howItWorks: The middle cell is wired in series between the other two, so the pack's voltage is the sum of all three. Every cell carries the same current, so if one is weaker than its neighbours it runs low first, and the management board watches it individually.
keyNumbers: Energy density roughly 200 to 260 Wh per kg
Weighs roughly 70 to 100 g
Lasts typically a few hundred full cycles
details.madeOf: Like its neighbours, a lithium-polymer pouch: coated metal foils, a porous separator and gel electrolyte inside an aluminium-plastic laminate.

parts.name: Lithium-polymer cell 2

parts.description: One of three pouch cells in series, about 11.4 V together and good for roughly half an hour of flight.

details.didYouKnow: Drones typically trigger a return-to-home well before the battery is flat, because they calculate how much energy they need to fly back against the wind.
details.howItWorks: The top cell of the stack provides the pack's positive terminal. During a flight the cells' voltage slowly sags from about 4.4 V towards roughly 3.3 V each, and the drone uses that curve, with current measurements, to estimate how many minutes of flight remain.
keyNumbers: Discharged to no lower than about 3.0 to 3.3 V
Charges fully in roughly an hour
Cells matched to within a few millivolts when built
details.madeOf: A lithium-polymer pouch cell; the 'polymer' refers to the gel electrolyte and flat soft pack rather than any special chemistry.

parts.name: Lithium-polymer cell 3

parts.description: Balances the cells, tracks charge and cuts power if the pack overheats or over-discharges.

details.didYouKnow: The smart battery keeps its own log of cycles and faults, so a drone can refuse a pack that the board has flagged as damaged.
details.howItWorks: The battery management board measures each cell's voltage, the pack's temperature and the current flowing in and out, and counts charge like a fuel gauge. It balances the cells by bleeding a little energy from any that run high, and it talks to the drone so the app can show exact percentage, cycle count and health.
keyNumbers: Monitors each of the 3 cells separately
Cuts off if cells reach roughly 60 degrees C or more
Self-discharges to about 60 percent after several days unused
details.madeOf: A small printed circuit board with a battery-monitor chip, current-sense resistor, temperature sensors and protection MOSFETs that can cut the output.

parts.name: Battery management board

parts.description: Main computer: fuses the sensors and adjusts each motor hundreds of times a second to hold the drone steady.

details.didYouKnow: A quadcopter cannot be flown by hand without a computer in the loop; it is naturally unstable, and the controller makes hundreds of tiny corrections every second.
details.howItWorks: The flight controller runs the control loops that keep the drone stable: it combines readings from the IMU, compass, GPS, vision sensors and barometer into one estimate of position and attitude, compares it with what the pilot wants, and sends new speed commands to each of the four motors. To move forward, for example, it slows the front motors slightly and speeds up the rear ones so the craft tilts.
keyNumbers: Inner stabilising loop runs roughly 1,000 times a second or more
Typically 4 to 8 board layers
Holds position to within roughly 0.5 m with GPS
details.madeOf: A multilayer fibreglass circuit board carrying a multi-core processor, memory and a barometer, often sharing space with the video and radio chips.

parts.name: Flight controller board

parts.description: Gyroscopes and accelerometers on a vibration-damped mount; they sense every tilt and jolt.

details.didYouKnow: The same kind of MEMS sensor that steadies a drone is what rotates your phone's screen when you turn it sideways.
details.howItWorks: The IMU contains microscopic vibrating structures that sense rotation (gyroscopes) and tiny springy masses that sense acceleration, including the pull of gravity. The flight controller blends the two so it always knows which way is down and how fast the drone is tilting. It sits on a soft mount so motor vibration does not drown out the real motion.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 gyro axes and 3 accelerometer axes
Samples roughly 1,000 to 8,000 times a second
Chip only about 3 mm across
details.madeOf: MEMS sensor chips etched from silicon, in a small package on a rubber- or foam-damped board, often with a backup IMU for redundancy.

parts.name: Inertial measurement unit

parts.description: Ceramic patch antenna and magnetometer that tell the drone where it is and which way it faces.

details.didYouKnow: Many drones use GPS together with GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou, so even if one system is poorly placed overhead there are plenty of satellites in view.
details.howItWorks: The square ceramic patch antenna picks up signals from satellites in several navigation systems, and the receiver works out position from tiny differences in their arrival times. The magnetometer beside it senses the Earth's magnetic field to give heading. The module sits high and away from motors and power wires so their magnetic noise does not disturb the compass.
keyNumbers: Usually tracks about 10 to 30 satellites
Position accuracy typically within a few metres
Updates about 5 to 10 times a second
details.madeOf: A ceramic patch antenna, whose high dielectric constant lets it be small, plus a receiver chip and a MEMS magnetometer on a shielded board.

parts.name: GPS and compass module

parts.description: Finned block that pulls heat from the video processor.

details.didYouKnow: If a drone is left powered on the ground on a hot day it may show an overheating warning, because there is no propeller airflow to help cool it.
details.howItWorks: The heat sink sits pressed against the main processor through a thermal pad, soaking up heat and spreading it across many thin fins. The fan blows air between the fins to carry the heat out through the shell vents. In flight the downwash from the propellers helps, which is why the drone can run hotter while sitting on the ground.
keyNumbers: Aluminium conducts heat about 1,000 times better than plastic
Processor may produce several watts of heat
Fins typically about 0.5 to 1 mm thick
details.madeOf: Extruded or die-cast aluminium, which conducts heat well, is light and easy to form into thin fins.

parts.name: Heat sink

parts.description: Small blower that pushes air across the heat sink.

details.didYouKnow: Some drones keep their fan running for a short while after landing, to clear heat soaked into the body.
details.howItWorks: The fan is a tiny brushless blower that draws air in through the vents, pushes it across the heat sink fins and out the other side. The flight controller can vary its speed with temperature, running it harder when the video processor is busy recording high-resolution footage.
keyNumbers: Typically about 15 to 25 mm across
Spins at roughly 10,000 rpm or more
Draws well under 1 W
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic impeller and housing around a miniature brushless motor, chosen to keep it light and quiet.

parts.name: Cooling fan

parts.description: Camera that watches the ground so the drone can hold position indoors without GPS.

details.didYouKnow: Optical flow struggles over plain or reflective surfaces like still water, white floors or snow, because there is no texture to track.
details.howItWorks: The downward cameras film the ground and track how patterns of texture slide across the image, a technique called optical flow, to work out how the drone is drifting. The flight controller then corrects for it, letting the drone hover steadily indoors or under trees where GPS is weak. With two cameras it can also judge height by stereo.
keyNumbers: Typically works from about 0.5 to 10 m above ground
Images captured roughly 30 to 60 times a second
Low-resolution sensors, often under 1 megapixel
details.madeOf: A small CMOS image sensor behind a glass or plastic lens, usually a global-shutter black-and-white sensor because it captures fast motion without distortion.

parts.name: Downward vision sensor

parts.description: Time-of-flight sensor measuring the distance to the ground for smooth landings.

details.didYouKnow: The barometer in the drone measures air pressure to estimate height too, but close to the ground the infrared sensor is far more precise.
details.howItWorks: The time-of-flight sensor sends out pulses of invisible infrared light and times how long the reflection takes to return from the ground. Since light travels so fast, it measures delays of billionths of a second to give height, which helps with gentle, controlled landings and low-level hovering.
keyNumbers: Useful range typically up to about 8 to 10 m
Light travels about 30 cm in one nanosecond
Accuracy roughly a few centimetres
details.madeOf: An infrared laser or LED emitter and a light-sensitive detector chip behind an infrared-transparent window.

parts.name: Infrared height sensor

parts.description: One of a stereo pair that judges distance to obstacles ahead.

details.didYouKnow: Stereo depth works just like your own eyes: cover one eye and you will find threading a needle much harder.
details.howItWorks: This is the left eye of a stereo camera pair. The processor compares its image with the right camera's and measures how far each object appears to shift between the two; nearby objects shift more, which gives distance. That depth map lets the drone brake or steer around obstacles ahead.
keyNumbers: Detects obstacles typically up to about 20 to 40 m ahead
Field of view roughly 60 to 90 degrees
Lenses spaced a few centimetres apart
details.madeOf: A small global-shutter image sensor behind a wide-angle glass lens, mounted rigidly so its alignment with its partner never changes.

parts.name: Forward obstacle camera (left)

parts.description: One of a stereo pair that judges distance to obstacles ahead.

details.didYouKnow: Vision obstacle sensing generally does not work in darkness or against thin wires and bare branches, which is why pilots are told not to rely on it.
details.howItWorks: The right camera is the second half of the stereo pair. Its separation from the left camera, called the baseline, decides how far out the system can judge depth accurately. The two are calibrated in the factory, and the drone can use them for features like following a subject or mapping obstacles.
keyNumbers: Depth error grows roughly with the square of distance
Processed typically about 20 to 30 times a second
Works best in light above roughly 15 lux
details.madeOf: A matched image sensor and lens identical to the left one, since the two images must be as alike as possible for the comparison to work.

parts.name: Forward obstacle camera (right)

parts.description: Plate hung on rubber balls that isolates the camera from motor vibration.

details.didYouKnow: Without damping, motor vibration can cause a wobbly 'jello' effect in video, because the image sensor reads out each frame line by line.
details.howItWorks: The damper plate is the bridge between the airframe and the gimbal. It hangs from soft rubber balls, so the high-frequency buzz of the motors and propellers is absorbed before it reaches the camera, while the gimbal motors handle the slower movements like tilting and turning.
keyNumbers: Usually hung on about 3 to 4 dampers
Filters vibrations above roughly 100 Hz well
Weighs only a few grams
details.madeOf: A stiff moulded plastic or composite plate, light so it does not add inertia, but rigid so the gimbal's base does not twist.

parts.name: Gimbal damper plate

parts.description: One of the soft rubber isolators the gimbal hangs from.

details.didYouKnow: Rubber dampers harden and crack with age and sunlight, and swapping them is one of the cheapest fixes for shaky drone footage.
details.howItWorks: Each damper ball acts as a tiny spring and shock absorber in one: it squashes and recovers to soak up vibration, and its softness is tuned so the camera is isolated from buzz but not left swinging loosely. Its hollow shape lets it compress in every direction.
keyNumbers: Typically about 5 to 10 mm across
Shore hardness roughly 30 to 50A, fairly soft
Each weighs well under 1 g
details.madeOf: Soft silicone or similar rubber, chosen because it stays springy across hot and cold temperatures and damps energy well.

parts.name: Rubber damper ball

parts.description: Brushless motor that pans the camera left and right.

details.didYouKnow: Gimbal motors are designed for very smooth, slow movement, so they use many magnet poles and are driven with smooth sine-wave current rather than sharp pulses.
details.howItWorks: The yaw motor turns the whole camera assembly left and right. It mostly smooths out small twitches as the drone holds heading in wind, and on some drones it lets the camera pan independently of the body. Like the drone's own motors it is brushless, but it is driven to hold precise angles rather than spin fast.
keyNumbers: Usually turns through about 60 to 90 degrees
Holds angle to within roughly 0.01 degrees
Motor about 1 to 2 cm across
details.madeOf: A small brushless motor with copper windings, neodymium magnets and a steel housing, with an angle sensor so the controller always knows its exact position.

parts.name: Gimbal yaw motor

parts.description: L-shaped arm linking the yaw, roll and pitch motors.

details.didYouKnow: Gimbal arms are a common breaking point in a crash, so many drones are shipped with a clip-on gimbal guard for transport.
details.howItWorks: The gimbal arm links the three motors so each one rotates the camera about a different axis. Its L-shape keeps the axes crossing near the camera's centre of mass, which means the motors only need tiny forces to hold or move it.
keyNumbers: Links 3 rotation axes
Typically weighs about 5 to 15 g
Wall thickness roughly 1 mm
details.madeOf: A thin aluminium or titanium alloy arm, sometimes magnesium, picked for stiffness at very low weight so it does not flex or resonate.

parts.name: Gimbal arm

parts.description: Keeps the horizon level as the drone banks.

details.didYouKnow: On some drones you can tilt the roll axis on purpose to film in portrait orientation for social media.
details.howItWorks: When the drone banks to turn or fights a gust, the roll motor rotates the camera the opposite way so the horizon stays level in the shot. It responds to the gimbal's own IMU, mounted behind the camera, correcting within milliseconds.
keyNumbers: Corrects typically about plus or minus 30 to 45 degrees
Responds within a few milliseconds
Draws well under 1 W while holding
details.madeOf: A compact brushless motor with copper windings, rare-earth magnets and a magnetic angle sensor.

parts.name: Gimbal roll motor

parts.description: Tilts the camera up and down, and cancels the drone's nose-down lean in forward flight.

details.didYouKnow: A straight-down shot from a drone is so popular it has its own name, the 'top-down' or 'god's-eye' view.
details.howItWorks: The pitch motor tilts the camera up and down, letting the pilot look straight down for overhead shots or towards the horizon. In forward flight the whole drone leans nose-down, so this motor tilts the camera back up to keep the framing steady.
keyNumbers: Tilts typically from about 90 degrees down to around 20 to 35 degrees up
Holds steady to within about 0.01 degrees
Forward flight lean can reach roughly 30 degrees
details.madeOf: A small brushless motor with copper windings, neodymium magnets and an angle sensor, built into the camera's side mount.

parts.name: Gimbal pitch motor

parts.description: Sealed housing for the sensor and lens, balanced so the gimbal motors barely have to work.

details.didYouKnow: A well-balanced camera stays roughly where you point it even with the gimbal unpowered, which is exactly what designers aim for.
details.howItWorks: The housing holds the image sensor, lens and image-processing link at exactly the right spacing, and is balanced so its centre of mass sits on the gimbal's axes. A flexible flat cable runs out of it through the gimbal to carry video data to the main processor.
keyNumbers: Camera and gimbal together typically about 30 to 70 g
Video data rate up to roughly 150 to 200 Mbps
Often sealed against dust
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic, sometimes with a metal internal frame, kept as light as possible because every gram makes the gimbal motors work harder.

parts.name: Camera housing

parts.description: One-inch-class CMOS sensor that records 4K video.

details.didYouKnow: A 'one-inch' sensor is not one inch across; the name comes from old video camera tubes, and the actual diagonal is about 16 mm.
details.howItWorks: The image sensor is a grid of millions of light-sensitive pixels, each turning light into an electrical charge. A colour filter pattern over the pixels means each senses red, green or blue, and the processor combines neighbours to rebuild a full-colour image, many times a second for video.
keyNumbers: Active area roughly 13 by 9 mm for a one-inch-class sensor
Typically about 20 megapixels
Records 4K video at up to about 60 frames per second
details.madeOf: A silicon chip made by the CMOS process used for computer chips, with microlenses and colour filters printed on top of each pixel.

parts.name: Image sensor

parts.description: Holds the stack of glass elements at a fixed focus distance.

details.didYouKnow: Some drone cameras have an adjustable aperture, letting the pilot control exposure like a full-size camera instead of relying only on shutter speed and filters.
details.howItWorks: The barrel holds a stack of several lens elements at precise spacings, so together they focus light sharply onto the sensor and correct for colour fringing and distortion. Many drone cameras focus automatically by shifting elements, while others use a fixed setting that keeps everything from a few metres to the horizon sharp.
keyNumbers: Typically about 6 to 9 lens elements
Aperture commonly around f/2.8
Alignment tolerances of a few microns
details.madeOf: A machined or stamped metal tube, often aluminium or steel, sometimes with plastic spacers; metal holds the optical alignment even as temperatures change.

parts.name: Lens barrel

parts.description: Coated wide-angle glass, roughly a 24 mm equivalent view.

details.didYouKnow: Pilots often clip small ND filters over the front lens, like sunglasses, so they can use slower shutter speeds for natural-looking motion blur.
details.howItWorks: The front element is the first glass light passes through, bending it inwards so a wide scene fits onto the small sensor. Its multilayer coating reduces reflections and flare from the sun, and it also seals the front of the camera against dust and moisture.
keyNumbers: About a 24 mm equivalent focal length
Field of view roughly 80 to 85 degrees
Coatings cut reflection to under about 1 percent per surface
details.madeOf: Optical glass with thin anti-reflective coatings applied in a vacuum chamber, chosen for clarity and scratch resistance over plastic.

parts.name: Front lens element

summary: A folding camera quadcopter, modelled on drones like the DJI Mavic: four brushless motors and propellers, a three-axis stabilised camera, a smart battery, and the flight computer and sensors that keep it hovering in place.

name: Mechanical Watch
overview:
A mechanical watch keeps time with springs and gears and no battery. Everything is driven by one coiled mainspring. In an automatic watch like this one, a weighted rotor swings as you move your wrist and winds the spring for you; you can also wind it with the crown.

The mainspring unwinds through a gear train: a series of wheels, each turning faster than the last, that end at the escapement. On its own the spring would let go in seconds. The escapement makes it go slowly: an escape wheel is locked and released one tooth at a time by the pallet fork, which is rocked back and forth by the balance wheel. That release is the tick you hear.

The balance wheel and its hairspring are the actual timekeeper. Like a pendulum, they swing back and forth at a steady rate, here four times a second, and each swing in either direction lets the gear train advance one step: eight ticks a second. Gears off the train turn the minute hand once an hour and the hour hand once every twelve hours. Synthetic ruby jewels serve as nearly frictionless bearings.

parts.description: Synthetic sapphire window: almost as hard as diamond, so it shrugs off scratches.

details.didYouKnow: Synthetic sapphire is chemically the same stuff as ruby. The only difference is a trace of chromium, which turns it red, and that is exactly what the jewel bearings inside are made of.
details.howItWorks: The crystal is the clear front window that keeps fingers, dust and water off the hands. It is pressed into the bezel with a thin gasket around its edge, so it seals as well as protects. An anti-reflective coating on one or both faces stops glare from hiding the dial.
keyNumbers: Hardness: 9 on the Mohs scale (diamond is 10)
Thickness: typically about 1 to 2 mm
Melting point of sapphire: roughly 2,000 °C
details.madeOf: Synthetic sapphire, which is crystallised aluminium oxide grown in a furnace and then sliced, ground and polished with diamond tools. Nothing softer than diamond can cut it, which is why it stays clear for decades.

parts.name: Sapphire crystal

parts.description: Polished ring that clamps the crystal onto the case.

details.didYouKnow: On dive watches the bezel rotates one way only and carries a minute scale, so a diver can time their air supply without any risk of a bump making the dive look shorter.
details.howItWorks: The bezel is the ring around the crystal that holds it down against the case. On a dress watch like this one it is usually a tight press fit, snapped on with a hand press so the crystal and its gasket are squeezed into a watertight seal. Its polished slopes also frame the dial and catch the light.
keyNumbers: Outer diameter: about 40 mm, matching the case
Press-fit force: up to a few hundred newtons
Polishing: often several stages from coarse to mirror
details.madeOf: Usually the same 316L stainless steel as the case, machined on a CNC lathe and then polished by hand on buffing wheels so it matches the case finish.

parts.name: Bezel

parts.description: Stainless-steel ring that the movement sits in; the lugs for the strap are part of it.

details.didYouKnow: A 100 m water-resistance rating is a pressure test in a lab, not a promise you can dive to 100 m. Swinging your arm through water can briefly push the pressure well above the static figure.
details.howItWorks: The case middle is the main body of the watch. The movement sits inside it on a spacer ring, the bezel and crystal close the front, the case back screws into the rear, and the crown passes through a sealed tube in its side. Because the lugs are part of the same piece, every pull on the strap is taken by this one solid block of steel.
keyNumbers: Diameter: about 40 mm
Thickness: typically about 10 to 13 mm with crystal and back
Water resistance: typically 50 to 100 m rated
details.madeOf: Most steel watches use 316L stainless steel, an alloy with chromium, nickel and molybdenum that resists sweat and seawater. The case is usually forged or stamped roughly to shape, then CNC machined and polished.

parts.name: Case

parts.description: Horn that holds one end of a spring bar.

details.didYouKnow: Lug-to-lug length often matters more than case diameter for comfort: if the lugs overhang the edges of your wrist, even a small watch can look and feel too big.
details.howItWorks: Each lug is a horn sticking out from the case, and each pair of lugs has small holes drilled on their inner faces. The spring bar's tips snap into those holes, so the strap is held between the lugs. Their length and curve decide how well the watch hugs your wrist.
keyNumbers: Gap between lugs: typically about 20 mm on a 40 mm watch
Spring-bar holes: roughly 1 mm across
Lug-to-lug length: usually about 46 to 50 mm
details.madeOf: The lugs are machined out of the same stainless steel block as the case, so there are no joints to loosen or corrode.

parts.name: Lug

parts.description: Horn that holds one end of a spring bar.

details.didYouKnow: Early wristwatches were often converted pocket watches with wire loops soldered on for a strap. Built-in lugs became standard as wristwatches took over in the early twentieth century.
details.howItWorks: This lug pairs with its neighbour to grip a spring bar from both ends, which in turn carries one half of the strap. The steel has to cope with sudden tugs, such as catching the strap on a door handle, without bending. Some watches drill the holes right through the lug so a strap can be changed with a pin pushed from outside.
keyNumbers: Hole depth: typically about 1 mm
Usual lug widths: about 18, 20 or 22 mm
Lugs per watch: 4, two at each end
details.madeOf: Solid stainless steel, part of the one-piece case, usually given the same brushed or polished finish so the lines flow from case to strap.

parts.name: Lug

parts.description: Spring-loaded pin that snaps between the lugs to hold the strap.

details.didYouKnow: The little shoulder near each end of a spring bar is there for a forked tool to catch on, which is how a watchmaker compresses it in seconds.
details.howItWorks: A spring bar is a little tube with a pin poking out of each end and a coil spring inside pushing them apart. You squeeze the pins in, slide the bar between the lugs, and let them pop out into the lug holes. The strap's end loop wraps around the bar, so it carries all the strap's load.
keyNumbers: Tube diameter: typically about 1.5 to 1.8 mm
Tip diameter: roughly 0.8 to 1 mm
Length: matches the lug gap, often 20 mm
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube with hardened steel pins and a tiny steel spring, chosen so the bar stays strong and springy without rusting from sweat.

parts.name: Spring bar

parts.description: One half of the strap.

details.didYouKnow: Water and sweat are leather's enemies, which is why a leather strap usually wears out long before the watch needs its first service.
details.howItWorks: The strap comes in two halves: one carries the buckle and the other the holes. Each end loops around a spring bar between the lugs. Leather is padded and stitched in layers so it flexes around the wrist but does not stretch out of shape.
keyNumbers: Width at the lugs: about 20 mm
Taper at the buckle: often about 16 to 18 mm
Typical lengths: roughly 75 mm and 115 mm halves
details.madeOf: Tanned calf leather is the classic choice, often with a softer lining and a filler layer glued and stitched together. Tanning makes the hide flexible and stops it rotting.

parts.name: Leather strap

parts.description: Knob for winding the mainspring by hand and, pulled out, setting the time.

details.didYouKnow: It is called the crown because on pocket watches it sat on top of the case at 12 o'clock, like a crown on a head.
details.howItWorks: Pushed in, turning the crown winds the mainspring through the keyless works inside the movement. Pulled out one click, it usually sets the date; pulled out fully, it moves the hands and on many movements stops the balance so you can set the seconds exactly. Rubber seals inside the crown and its tube keep water out at every position.
keyNumbers: Diameter: typically about 5 to 7 mm
Positions: usually 3 (wind, date, time)
Hand winding from empty: roughly 30 to 40 turns
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, machined and given a grippy knurled edge, with one or more rubber O-rings inside to seal against the case tube.

parts.name: Crown

parts.description: Thin shaft linking the crown to the winding and setting gears inside the movement.

details.didYouKnow: When a watch is cased, the watchmaker trims the stem to length by hand so the crown sits snugly against the case without pressing on the movement.
details.howItWorks: The stem runs from the crown through the case into the movement. A square section along it drives a sliding clutch wheel, which a lever shifts between the winding gears and the hand-setting gears as you pull the crown in and out. Pressing a small release lever lets the stem slide out, which is how a watchmaker lifts the movement from the case.
keyNumbers: Thickness: usually under 1 mm
Length: roughly 10 to 15 mm, cut to fit the case
Crown positions it selects: typically 3
details.madeOf: Hardened and tempered carbon or stainless steel, threaded at the outer end to screw into the crown. It must be stiff enough not to twist under winding torque.

parts.name: Winding stem

parts.description: Rubber O-ring that keeps water and dust out.

details.didYouKnow: Rubber gaskets slowly harden with age, which is why an old watch that was once water-resistant should be pressure tested before you swim in it.
details.howItWorks: The gasket is a ring of rubber sitting in a groove between the case middle and the case back. Screwing the back down squeezes it, so it fills every tiny gap and blocks water, dust and moisture. A thin smear of silicone grease helps it seal and stops it drying out.
keyNumbers: Cross-section: typically under 1 mm
Diameter: roughly 30 to 35 mm
Replacement: usually at every service, roughly every 5 years
details.madeOf: Usually nitrile rubber or another synthetic rubber, which stays springy for years and does not swell in sweat or skin oils.

parts.name: Case-back gasket

parts.description: Screw-down steel back that seals the case.

details.didYouKnow: Many automatic watches swap the steel back for one with a sapphire window, so you can watch the rotor swing and the balance tick.
details.howItWorks: The case back closes the rear of the case. It screws onto a fine thread in the case middle, crushing the gasket to make the seal. Notches around its edge let a watchmaker's case wrench grip it to open the watch for service.
keyNumbers: Thread pitch: fine, typically well under 1 mm
Turns to close: roughly 1 to 3
Wrench notches: often 6
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, machined and threaded, often with engraving or stamped markings such as the reference number and water rating.

parts.name: Case back

parts.description: Sweeps round in tiny steps, one for every tick of the escapement.

details.didYouKnow: That smooth sweep is how people tell a mechanical watch from a quartz one at a glance, since most quartz seconds hands jump just once a second.
details.howItWorks: The seconds hand is pressed onto the arbor of the fourth wheel, which turns once a minute. Because the escapement releases the train in small jumps, the hand moves in tiny steps rather than a true glide. A short tail on the back balances its weight so it does not drag on the gears.
keyNumbers: Steps per second: 8 at 28,800 vibrations per hour
Steps per minute: 480
Weight: only a few milligrams
details.madeOf: Thin brass or steel, stamped and painted or lacquered, kept extremely light so it does not upset the train or shake loose in a knock.

parts.name: Seconds hand

parts.description: Driven once round per hour by the centre wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Hands are simply pushed onto their tubes, so fitting them so they line up exactly at 12 o'clock is a delicate job done under magnification.
details.howItWorks: The minute hand sits on the cannon pinion, a tube that grips the centre wheel arbor by friction. When the watch runs, friction carries the hand round once an hour. When you set the time, the crown turns the cannon pinion and it simply slips on the arbor, so the train and balance are not dragged backwards.
keyNumbers: Turns: once per hour, 24 times a day
Length: about the radius of the minute track, roughly 15 to 18 mm here
Fit: pressed on, no screws
details.madeOf: Stamped or machined steel or brass, often polished or plated and sometimes filled with luminous paint.

parts.name: Minute hand

parts.description: Geared down twelve to one from the minute hand.

details.didYouKnow: The hour wheel only turns twice a day, so its teeth barely wear, but it is what triggers the date change at midnight.
details.howItWorks: The hour hand sits on the hour wheel, a tube that rides loosely around the cannon pinion. A small set of gears called the motion works takes the minute hand's speed down twelve times, usually in two steps through an intermediate minute wheel. The hour wheel also drives the date mechanism.
keyNumbers: Reduction from minute hand: 12 to 1
Turns: twice per day
Gear stages: usually 2
details.madeOf: Steel or brass like the minute hand, usually shorter and wider so you can tell them apart at a glance.

parts.name: Hour hand

parts.description: Applied polished index, one for each hour.

details.didYouKnow: Early glow-in-the-dark dials used radioactive radium paint. Today's lume is a non-radioactive pigment that soaks up light and slowly re-emits it.
details.howItWorks: Applied markers are small solid pieces fixed to the dial at each hour position. Tiny feet on their backs push through holes in the dial and are secured from behind. Their polished faces catch light from different angles, making the time easy to read without numbers.
keyNumbers: Count: 12, one per hour
Length: typically a few millimetres
Feet per marker: usually 1 or 2
details.madeOf: Usually brass or steel, cut and then diamond-polished, sometimes plated or filled with a strip of luminous pigment such as strontium aluminate.

parts.name: Hour marker

parts.description: Lacquered brass disc; two small feet on its back locate it on the movement.

details.didYouKnow: Dial text is applied by pad printing: a squishy silicone pad lifts ink from an etched plate and presses it onto the dial, letting lettering only a fraction of a millimetre tall come out crisp.
details.howItWorks: The dial is the face you read the time from. Feet on its back slot into holes in the main plate and are clamped by small screws, so it sits precisely around the hand arbors. A window cut in it lets you see the date ring underneath.
keyNumbers: Thickness: typically about 0.4 to 0.5 mm
Diameter: roughly 30 to 33 mm here
Feet: usually 2
details.madeOf: A thin brass disc, finished with lacquer, galvanic plating or a brushed sunburst, then printed with fine text using a soft silicone pad.

parts.name: Dial

parts.description: Ring printed 1 to 31 that a finger flicks forward one step at midnight.

details.didYouKnow: On many watches you should not set the date between roughly 9 pm and 3 am, because the date finger is already engaged and forcing it can damage the teeth.
details.howItWorks: The date ring sits just under the dial with 31 internal teeth. A finger on a wheel that turns once a day, driven by the hour wheel, catches a tooth around midnight and pushes it on by one, and a small sprung jumper snaps it neatly into place. Pulling the crown out one click lets you quickly step it forward by hand.
keyNumbers: Positions: 31
Advance: once every 24 hours
Manual corrections: about 5 times a year for short months
details.madeOf: A thin printed ring of metal or plastic, kept as light as possible so the small date finger can move it without stealing much power.

parts.name: Date ring

parts.description: Brass foundation of the movement: every wheel pivots in a jewel set into it or into a bridge.

details.didYouKnow: Watchmakers still measure movements in lignes, an old French unit of about 2.26 mm, so a common 11.5 ligne movement is about 26 mm across.
details.howItWorks: The main plate is the base of the movement. The wheels sit between it and the bridges above, with each pivot running in a jewel pressed into one or the other. Holes, recesses and threaded posts are machined into it so every part lines up to within a few thousandths of a millimetre.
keyNumbers: Diameter: typically about 25 to 30 mm
Machining tolerance: often a few microns
Movement size: around 11 to 13 lignes
details.madeOf: Brass, which machines cleanly and does not rust, usually plated with nickel or rhodium for a bright, stable finish and often decorated with tiny overlapping circles called perlage.

parts.name: Main plate

parts.description: Synthetic ruby bearing; hard and slick, so the steel pivots barely wear.

details.didYouKnow: Jewel bearings were patented in England in 1704, but they only became cheap after a French chemist found a way to grow synthetic rubies around 1900.
details.howItWorks: A jewel bearing is a tiny ruby with a polished hole that a steel pivot turns in. Ruby is so hard and smooth that friction stays low and the hole barely wears, even after billions of turns. A drop of special oil sits in a little cup on the jewel and is held there by surface tension.
keyNumbers: Jewels in a typical automatic: about 21 to 25
Hole size: roughly 0.1 to 0.2 mm
Hardness: 9 on the Mohs scale
details.madeOf: Synthetic ruby, which is lab-grown aluminium oxide with a trace of chromium. It is cheap to make, so jewels add durability rather than value.

parts.name: Jewel bearing

parts.description: Toothed rim of the barrel; it turns slowly as the spring unwinds and drives the whole train.

details.didYouKnow: Watch gears do not use the involute tooth shape found in car gearboxes. They use curves borrowed from cycloids, which work better with the tiny pinions that watches need.
details.howItWorks: The teeth around the barrel mesh with the pinion of the centre wheel. As the mainspring inside slowly unwinds, it turns the whole barrel, and these teeth hand that torque on to the rest of the gear train. They carry the highest force and turn the slowest of any wheel in the train.
keyNumbers: Speed: only a handful of turns per day
Ratio down to the escape wheel: several thousand to one
Torque: highest in the whole train
details.madeOf: Brass or a hard copper alloy, with teeth cut on a gear-hobbing machine so they mesh smoothly with the steel pinion.

parts.name: Barrel teeth

parts.description: Drum holding the mainspring — the watch's fuel tank, good for about two days.

details.didYouKnow: Because the spring slips inside the barrel when full, you can wind an automatic by hand as long as you like without breaking anything.
details.howItWorks: The barrel is a closed drum with the mainspring coiled inside.
