keyNumbers: EU drive-by noise limits for cars about 68 to 70 dB(A)
Gas cools to roughly 100 to 300 degrees C by here
Typically 5 to 10 kg
details.madeOf: Stainless or aluminised steel shell and baffles, sometimes stuffed with glass or mineral wool. Stainless lasts longer against condensation, which collects in the silencer at the back.

parts.name: Silencer

parts.description: Moulded plastic tank under the rear seat holding about 50 litres of petrol.

details.didYouKnow: The fuel pump sits submerged in the petrol, which cools it, and that is one reason running regularly on nearly empty can shorten its life.
details.howItWorks: The tank sits under the rear seat, inside the wheelbase, where it is best protected in a crash. An electric pump inside it sends fuel forward to the engine through a filter, and a float sender measures the level for the gauge. Petrol vapour is collected in a charcoal canister and later drawn into the engine to be burnt instead of escaping.
keyNumbers: About 50 litres
A full tank weighs roughly 37 kg of petrol
Range typically 700 to 900 km
Pump pressure about 3 to 5 bar
details.madeOf: Blow-moulded high-density polyethylene in several layers, including a thin barrier layer that stops petrol vapour seeping through. Plastic can be moulded into awkward shapes to fill every space and does not rust.

parts.name: Fuel tank

parts.description: 205/55 R16 radial tyre; its contact patch with the road is about the size of a postcard.

details.didYouKnow: On front-wheel-drive cars the front tyres usually wear out roughly twice as fast as the rears, which is why some people swap them front to back.
details.howItWorks: This tyre steers, drives and does much of the braking, so it works hardest of all four. It sits under the driver's corner, near the gearbox and battery, so it carries a little more weight than the right front. The code 205/55 R16 means 205 mm wide, a sidewall 55% as tall as that width, radial construction and a 16-inch wheel.
keyNumbers: About 632 mm overall diameter
Typically 2.2 to 2.5 bar
New tread about 8 mm; legal minimum 1.6 mm in the UK and EU
Roughly 8 to 9 kg
details.madeOf: Natural and synthetic rubber with carbon black and silica, over steel belts and polyester cords. Silica improves wet grip and lowers rolling resistance.

parts.name: Tyre (front left)

parts.description: Cast aluminium wheel bolted to the hub with five nuts.

details.didYouKnow: Wheel nuts should be tightened in a star pattern rather than round in a circle so the wheel pulls evenly against the hub.
details.howItWorks: The wheel holds the tyre and transfers all of its loads to the hub on five studs and nuts. Through its open spokes you can see the front brake disc and caliper, and the openings let air in to cool them. Being a driven and steered wheel, it carries braking, cornering and drive torque all at once.
keyNumbers: 16 inches by about 6.5 inches
Roughly 8 to 10 kg
Nuts typically tightened to about 110 to 120 Nm
Five-stud pitch typically 100 to 115 mm
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium alloy, usually low-pressure cast then machined and painted or lacquered. Aluminium is lighter than steel, which reduces unsprung weight and helps the suspension follow the road.

parts.name: Alloy wheel (front left)

parts.description: Iron disc that turns with the wheel; the caliper's pads grip it to stop the car.

details.didYouKnow: Many cars split their brakes diagonally, front left with rear right, so if one circuit leaks the car can still stop in a straight line on the other.
details.howItWorks: When the pedal is pressed, the caliper's pads squeeze this disc and friction turns the car's motion into heat. Front discs do most of the stopping because braking shifts weight onto the nose, so they are bigger and ventilated: two faces with cooling vanes between them that pump air outwards as the disc spins. This left disc is on the same hydraulic circuit as the right rear brake.
keyNumbers: About 280 mm across
Typically 22 to 25 mm thick
Up to about 500 degrees C in hard braking
Roughly 6 to 8 kg
details.madeOf: Grey cast iron, which handles high temperatures, wears evenly against the pads and damps vibration. Its carbon content helps conduct heat away from the surface.

parts.name: Brake disc (front left)

parts.description: Hydraulic clamp holding the brake pads either side of the disc.

details.didYouKnow: Brake fluid absorbs water from the air over time, lowering its boiling point, which is why it should be changed roughly every two years.
details.howItWorks: Brake fluid pushed from the master cylinder forces a large piston out of this caliper, pressing the inner pad onto the disc. The caliper body floats on two slide pins, so it pulls the outer pad against the other face at the same time. When the pedal is released, the piston seal draws the piston back very slightly so the pads stop dragging.
keyNumbers: Single piston about 54 to 57 mm across
Hydraulic pressure up to about 100 bar in an emergency stop
Pads typically last 30,000 to 60,000 km
details.madeOf: A cast iron body and bracket with a steel or phenolic piston, painted for corrosion protection. Pads are a friction compound of fibres, metals and resins bonded to a steel backing plate.

parts.name: Brake caliper (front left)

parts.description: MacPherson strut: a damper inside a coil spring that also locates and steers the wheel.

details.didYouKnow: The strut is named after Earle MacPherson, the engineer who developed it, and it first appeared in a production car on the British Ford Consul around 1950.
details.howItWorks: The MacPherson strut combines the damper and spring in one unit that bolts to the hub at the bottom and to the body at the top, where a bearing lets it rotate when the wheel steers. The damper forces oil through small valves as the wheel moves, turning bouncing energy into heat so the car settles after a bump. A lower control arm locates the bottom of the hub, and the steering rack's track rod pushes on an arm on the strut.
keyNumbers: Wheel travel roughly 150 to 200 mm in total
Typically 4 to 6 kg without the spring
Dampers often last about 100,000 km
details.madeOf: A steel tube filled with oil and often pressurised nitrogen gas, with a chrome-plated steel piston rod. The top mount uses rubber to isolate road noise from the body.

parts.name: Front strut (left)

parts.description: Carries the car's weight at the front corner and lets the wheel rise over bumps.

details.didYouKnow: Left and right springs are sometimes made to slightly different heights so the car sits level despite the driver and heavy parts being on one side.
details.howItWorks: The spring wraps around the strut and holds up the front left corner, compressing when the wheel hits a bump and pushing it back down afterwards. It carries the weight of the driver plus the gearbox and battery on this side. The damper inside controls how quickly the spring rebounds, so the car does not keep bouncing.
keyNumbers: Rate roughly 20 to 30 N/mm
Carries roughly 350 to 450 kg
Typically 5 to 7 coils
Bounce frequency about 1 to 1.5 Hz
details.madeOf: Silicon-chromium spring steel wire, hot or cold coiled, heat treated and shot-peened to resist fatigue, then powder-coated against rust.

parts.name: Front coil spring (left)

parts.description: 205/55 R16 radial tyre; its contact patch with the road is about the size of a postcard.

details.didYouKnow: A bulge in the sidewall after hitting a kerb means the internal cords have broken, and the tyre needs replacing even if it still holds air.
details.howItWorks: The right front tyre steers and drives like the left, and is under the engine side of the car. On a left-hand-drive car in right-hand traffic it runs on the kerb side, so it is the one most likely to be scraped against kerbs and to drop into gutters and drains. Pumped to the right pressure, its contact patch is roughly postcard sized.
keyNumbers: About 205 mm wide
Sidewall about 113 mm tall
Roughly 500 turns per km
Speed rating typically up to 190 to 240 km/h
details.madeOf: Rubber compounds over steel belts and fabric cords. The sidewall is thinner and more flexible than the tread, which is why kerb damage there is dangerous.

parts.name: Tyre (front right)

parts.description: Cast aluminium wheel bolted to the hub with five nuts.

details.didYouKnow: Kerbed alloy wheels are so common that there is a whole trade of mobile wheel refurbishers who repair them at the roadside.
details.howItWorks: The right front wheel mirrors the left, driven by the longer right driveshaft and steered by the rack. On the kerb side it is the wheel most likely to collect scuffs on its rim. It is centred on the hub by a machined spigot, while the five nuts clamp it tight.
keyNumbers: 16 inches in diameter
Roughly 8 to 10 kg
Offset typically about 40 to 50 mm
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium alloy, machined at the hub face and bead seats so the tyre seals and the wheel runs true.

parts.name: Alloy wheel (front right)

parts.description: Iron disc that turns with the wheel; the caliper's pads grip it to stop the car.

details.didYouKnow: Discs usually have their minimum safe thickness stamped on the edge or hub, so a mechanic can measure and tell when they need replacing.
details.howItWorks: Like the left, this ventilated disc spins with the wheel and does a large share of the stopping. Together the two front brakes do roughly two thirds or more of the braking work. This right disc shares a hydraulic circuit with the left rear brake in a diagonal split, so the car always keeps one front brake if a circuit fails.
keyNumbers: About 280 mm across
Typically 22 to 25 mm thick
Minimum thickness usually stamped on the disc
details.madeOf: Grey cast iron, cast with internal cooling vanes and machined flat. Some discs have a coating on the hub area to stop it rusting visibly through the wheel.

parts.name: Brake disc (front right)

parts.description: Hydraulic clamp holding the brake pads either side of the disc.

details.didYouKnow: A squeal when braking is often the pad wear indicator, a small metal tab designed to scrape on the disc and make noise when the pad is worn down.
details.howItWorks: This floating caliper squeezes the right front disc whenever the brakes are applied. The ABS unit can pulse its pressure many times a second if this wheel starts to lock, and the stability control can brake it on its own to help pull the car back into line. A small wear sensor wire may be clipped into its pad to warn when the pad is thin.
keyNumbers: Single piston about 54 to 57 mm across
ABS can pulse roughly 10 to 15 times a second
Pads about 10 to 12 mm thick when new
details.madeOf: Cast iron housing with steel slide pins in rubber boots, and pads of bonded friction material on steel backing plates.

parts.name: Brake caliper (front right)

parts.description: MacPherson strut: a damper inside a coil spring that also locates and steers the wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Replacing a strut changes the front wheel alignment, so the tracking usually needs setting afterwards to stop uneven tyre wear.
details.howItWorks: The right strut mirrors the left, holding the right front hub and steering with it. Being under the engine side and on the kerb side, it bears a bit more weight and tends to take more of the hard knocks from drains and potholes near the edge of the road. Its top bolts into a strut tower inside the engine bay, which the body is reinforced around.
keyNumbers: Usually 2 or 3 top-mount bolts
Wheel travel roughly 150 to 200 mm
Typically 4 to 6 kg without the spring
details.madeOf: A steel tube damper with oil and gas inside, chrome-plated piston rod and rubber top mount. The steel hub knuckle bolts to its base.

parts.name: Front strut (right)

parts.description: Carries the car's weight at the front corner and lets the wheel rise over bumps.

details.didYouKnow: Springs tend to sag slightly over many years, so replacing them in pairs keeps the car level side to side.
details.howItWorks: The right front spring holds up the corner beneath the engine. It works with the left spring and an anti-roll bar that links the two sides, so when the car leans in a corner the outer spring is helped by the bar to resist body roll. Both front springs are stiffer than the rears because the nose carries more of the weight.
keyNumbers: Rate roughly 20 to 30 N/mm
Carries roughly 350 to 450 kg
Front axle carries about 60% of the car's weight
details.madeOf: Heat-treated, shot-peened silicon-chromium spring steel with a protective coating. Spring steel can be compressed millions of times without losing its shape.

parts.name: Front coil spring (right)

parts.description: 205/55 R16 radial tyre; its contact patch with the road is about the size of a postcard.

details.didYouKnow: Tyre makers advise fitting the best pair of tyres on the rear, even on front-wheel-drive cars, because a loss of rear grip is harder for drivers to control.
details.howItWorks: The rear tyres do not drive or steer on this car, but they keep the back end stable in corners and under braking. With most of the weight over the nose, the rear left tyre carries less load, so its tread wears more slowly. Rear tyre grip matters most in a sudden swerve: if the rears lose grip before the fronts, the car can spin.
keyNumbers: Typically 2.0 to 2.4 bar
Carries roughly 250 to 300 kg
Often lasts 50,000 km or more on this car
details.madeOf: Rubber compounds over steel belts and polyester cords, identical to the front tyres so they can be swapped around.

parts.name: Tyre (rear left)

parts.description: Cast aluminium wheel bolted to the hub with five nuts.

details.didYouKnow: On many modern cars the rear wheel bearing comes as a sealed hub unit that is replaced whole rather than cleaned and regreased.
details.howItWorks: The rear left wheel is bolted to a hub that spins on a sealed bearing fixed to the twist-beam axle. It carries only braking and cornering loads, not drive. The rear brake caliper and smaller disc sit behind its spokes.
keyNumbers: 16 inches in diameter
Roughly 8 to 10 kg
Five nuts at about 110 to 120 Nm
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium alloy, matching the fronts. The same wheel fits all four corners, which simplifies rotating the tyres.

parts.name: Alloy wheel (rear left)

parts.description: Iron disc that turns with the wheel; the caliper's pads grip it to stop the car.

details.didYouKnow: Rear discs on cars that brake gently can rust and score from lack of use, so occasional firm stops help keep them clean.
details.howItWorks: The rear disc helps stop the car and keeps it straight under braking, but takes much less of the work than the fronts. Electronic brake-force distribution reduces rear pressure when weight shifts forward, to stop the rear wheels locking first. This left rear disc is on the same diagonal circuit as the front right.
keyNumbers: About 250 to 270 mm across
Typically about 10 mm thick
Does roughly a third or less of the braking
details.madeOf: Grey cast iron, usually solid rather than ventilated because it does not get as hot. Its central hat area sometimes forms a small drum for the parking brake.

parts.name: Brake disc (rear left)

parts.description: Hydraulic clamp holding the brake pads either side of the disc.

details.didYouKnow: Cars with an electric parking brake often need a diagnostic tool or special button sequence to wind the rear pistons back for a pad change.
details.howItWorks: The rear caliper squeezes the rear disc hydraulically just like the fronts, with a smaller piston for less force. It also doubles as the parking brake: either a cable from the handbrake lever turns a screw mechanism behind the piston, or a small electric motor on the caliper winds it in when the parking brake button is pressed.
keyNumbers: Piston about 34 to 38 mm across
Pads typically last 50,000 km or more
Electric park brake motor typically takes about 1 second to apply
details.madeOf: A cast iron caliper with a steel piston and a built-in mechanical or motorised parking mechanism. Smaller pads than the fronts.

parts.name: Brake caliper (rear left)

parts.description: Supports the rear corner on the twist-beam axle.

details.didYouKnow: Rear springs are often deliberately a little stiffer per kilogram than the fronts, so the back of the car settles at a different rate and the body does not pitch on bumps.
details.howItWorks: The rear left spring sits between the twist-beam axle and the body, usually separate from the damper, which is mounted just behind it. Separating them leaves more room for the boot floor. It carries less weight than the front springs, but it has to cope with a load range from an empty car to one full of passengers and luggage.
keyNumbers: Rate roughly 20 to 35 N/mm
Carries roughly 250 to 350 kg
Rear axle carries about 40% of the car's weight
details.madeOf: Silicon-chromium spring steel, coiled, heat treated and coated. Rear springs are often shorter and barrel shaped to fit under the floor.

parts.name: Rear coil spring (left)

parts.description: 205/55 R16 radial tyre; its contact patch with the road is about the size of a postcard.

details.didYouKnow: A tyre's age matters as well as its tread: the rubber hardens over time, and a four-digit date code on the sidewall tells the week and year it was made.
details.howItWorks: The rear right tyre follows behind the front right, running on the kerb side in right-hand traffic. It carries the lightest load of the four, under the fuel tank side and away from the engine, and wears slowest. Like all modern tyres, it is a radial, with cords running straight across from bead to bead for flexible sidewalls and a flat, stable tread.
keyNumbers: About 205 mm wide on a 16 inch rim
Wear bars at about 1.6 mm
Roughly 8 to 9 kg
details.madeOf: Synthetic and natural rubber, steel belts, fabric cords and steel bead wires. Tread wear indicator bars moulded into the grooves show when it reaches the legal limit.

parts.name: Tyre (rear right)

parts.description: Cast aluminium wheel bolted to the hub with five nuts.

details.didYouKnow: Some tyre pressure warning systems have no pressure sensors at all; they compare wheel speeds, because a soft tyre has a slightly smaller rolling radius and spins faster.
details.howItWorks: The rear right wheel spins on a bearing at the right end of the twist-beam axle. Wheel speed sensors read a toothed ring or magnetic encoder at each hub, feeding the ABS, stability control and often the tyre pressure warning. On this side it is the most likely rear wheel to be kerbed when parking.
keyNumbers: 16 inches in diameter
Roughly 8 to 10 kg
Spins about 500 times per km
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium alloy, the same as the other three.

parts.name: Alloy wheel (rear right)

parts.description: Iron disc that turns with the wheel; the caliper's pads grip it to stop the car.

details.didYouKnow: Stability control can stop a car spinning by gently braking just one wheel, which creates a turning force that nudges the car back into line.
details.howItWorks: The right rear disc shares a hydraulic circuit with the front left brake in a diagonal split. It helps keep the back of the car stable under braking, and the stability control can brake it on its own to correct a slide. It is smaller and solid because the rear brakes see far less heat.
keyNumbers: About 250 to 270 mm across
Typically about 10 mm thick
Roughly 4 to 5 kg
details.madeOf: Grey cast iron, solid and machined flat, sometimes with a protective coating on the non-braking areas.

parts.name: Brake disc (rear right)

parts.description: Hydraulic clamp holding the brake pads either side of the disc.

details.didYouKnow: Holding the electric parking brake button while moving typically triggers a controlled stop using the main brakes, rather than locking the rear wheels.
details.howItWorks: This floating caliper clamps the right rear disc and, like the left one, holds the car still as the parking brake. With an electric parking brake, the motors at both rear calipers apply automatically when the engine is switched off on many cars, and can act as an emergency brake if the button is held while moving.
keyNumbers: Piston about 34 to 38 mm across
Parking brake must hold the car on roughly a 20% slope
Pads about 10 mm thick when new
details.madeOf: Cast iron with a steel piston, a rubber dust boot and slide pins, plus a parking mechanism inside. Pads are a friction compound on steel backing.

parts.name: Brake caliper (rear right)

parts.description: Supports the rear corner on the twist-beam axle.

details.didYouKnow: A broken coil spring often snaps right at the bottom coil where it sits in its seat, because salty water collects there and corrodes the steel.
details.howItWorks: The right rear spring supports the corner nearest the fuel tank on this car, so its load changes as the tank fills and empties. It sits on a pad on top of the twist-beam's trailing arm, with the damper mounted separately behind it. Together with the left spring it sets the ride height at the back.
keyNumbers: Rate roughly 20 to 35 N/mm
Load changes by up to about 37 kg from empty to full tank
Typically 4 to 6 coils
details.madeOf: Heat-treated silicon-chromium spring steel, coated against stones and salt, seated in rubber isolators to cut road noise.

parts.name: Rear coil spring (right)

parts.description: Steel beam linking the two rear wheels; it twists slightly so each side can move over bumps.

details.didYouKnow: The twist beam was popularised by mid-1970s Volkswagen and Audi models, and is still used on many small and mid-size cars because it is cheap, light and compact.
details.howItWorks: The twist beam is a U or V-shaped cross beam joining two trailing arms that carry the rear hubs. The front ends of the arms pivot on rubber bushes on the body. When one wheel rises, the cross beam twists, so the wheels can move semi-independently, and that twisting also works as a built-in anti-roll bar.
keyNumbers: Roughly 15 to 25 kg
Two main body bushes
Spans roughly 1.5 m between the wheel centres
details.madeOf: Pressed and welded steel, with the cross-beam section carefully shaped to give the right twisting stiffness. Rubber bushes isolate it from the body.

parts.name: Twist-beam rear axle

parts.description: Rack-and-pinion gear that turns the steering wheel's rotation into a sideways push on the front wheels.

details.didYouKnow: Electric power steering uses energy only when you steer, unlike older hydraulic systems whose pumps ran all the time, which saves a little fuel.
details.howItWorks: A small pinion gear on the end of the steering column meshes with teeth along a steel bar, the rack, so turning the wheel slides the rack left or right. Track rods with ball joints at each end push and pull the steering arms on the struts, swinging the front wheels. An electric motor adds assistance, and the car's computer can use it for lane-keeping and self-parking.
keyNumbers: Rack travel roughly 140 to 160 mm lock to lock
Turning circle about 10.5 to 11 m
Typically 2.5 to 3 steering wheel turns lock to lock
details.madeOf: A cast aluminium housing with a hardened steel rack and pinion, sealed by rubber gaiters and lubricated with grease.

parts.name: Steering rack

summary: A four-door family car with a 1.5-litre four-cylinder petrol engine driving the front wheels through a six-speed gearbox: around 1,300 kg of steel body, glass, wheels and machinery.

name: Light Helicopter
overview:
A helicopter is an aircraft that makes its own lift by spinning its wings. The main rotor blades are long, thin wings; as they whirl round they push air downwards, and that holds the helicopter up. Because the blades move even when the helicopter doesn't, it can take off straight up, hover in one spot and land almost anywhere.

The pilot steers by changing the angle of the blades. The collective lever changes all of them together for more or less lift, to climb or descend. The cyclic stick tilts the swashplate, a pair of plates under the rotor head, so each blade takes a bigger bite on one side of its circle than the other. That tilts the whole rotor disc and the helicopter moves that way.

Spinning the rotor one way pushes the body the other way, so a small tail rotor at the end of the boom pushes sideways to stop the helicopter spinning. The pedals change its pitch to turn left or right. A gas-turbine engine on the roof drives everything through the main gearbox, which slows its very fast turbine down to the rotor's few hundred rpm and sends power down a long shaft to the tail.

parts.description: Composite wing about 5 m long; its pitch is changed many times a second to steer the helicopter.

details.didYouKnow: At rest the long blades droop noticeably under their own weight; once spinning, the centrifugal pull straightens them out almost like a stiff rope being whirled.
details.howItWorks: Each blade is a long, narrow wing that makes lift as it sweeps round, and together the three blades carry the whole weight of the helicopter. The swashplate and pitch links twist each blade slightly once every turn, giving it more bite on one side of the circle than the other, which tilts the rotor disc and pulls the helicopter in that direction. The blades also flex upwards in flight, so the spinning disc forms a shallow cone rather than a flat circle.
keyNumbers: About 5 m long each
Tips moving at roughly 220 m/s, about 800 km/h
Pitch cycled about 6 to 7 times a second
Together they lift up to about 2,250 kg
details.madeOf: Glass and carbon fibre skins over a foam or honeycomb core, built around a strong spar, with a metal strip along the leading edge to resist erosion from rain and sand. Composites resist fatigue far better than the aluminium blades of older helicopters.

parts.name: Main rotor blade

parts.description: Fork that holds the root of each blade and lets it twist to change pitch.

details.didYouKnow: On many light helicopters, pulling out one of the two blade pins lets a blade swing round to lie along the fuselage, so the aircraft can fit into a smaller hangar.
details.howItWorks: The grip clamps the root of a blade with heavy bolts and connects it to the hub through a bearing that lets the blade rotate about its own long axis. A short arm on the grip, the pitch horn, is where the pitch link pushes and pulls to twist the blade. The grip has to hold the blade against an enormous outward pull while still letting it twist freely many times a second.
keyNumbers: Holds against an outward pull of roughly 15 tonnes or more
Usually two main bolts or pins per blade
Pitch range of roughly 20 degrees or so
details.madeOf: Forged and machined high-strength steel or titanium. Forging lines the metal's grain up with the loads, which matters for a part that is never allowed to crack.

parts.name: Blade grip

parts.description: Star-shaped hub on top of the mast that carries the blades and lets them flap up and down.

details.didYouKnow: Elastomeric bearings, stacks of thin rubber and steel layers, need no oil at all, which removed one of the biggest maintenance chores from rotor heads.
details.howItWorks: The hub joins the three blade grips to the top of the mast and has to allow each blade to flap up and down, lead and lag a little, and twist for pitch. On modern light helicopters these motions are taken up by flexible arms and elastomeric bearings instead of greased hinges. Flapping matters because the blade advancing into the wind makes more lift than the retreating one, and letting it rise evens the lift out across the disc.
keyNumbers: Turns at about 400 rpm
Carries three blades 120 degrees apart
Rotor disc of roughly 90 square metres
details.madeOf: Older hubs are forged and machined steel or titanium; many modern ones use a composite star with bearings made of bonded layers of rubber and metal. The composite flexes in a controlled way and shows damage gradually rather than snapping.

parts.name: Rotor hub

parts.description: Rod from the swashplate to a blade's pitch horn; pushing it up or down twists the blade.

details.didYouKnow: Adjusting the pitch links so the blades follow each other is called tracking; mechanics once checked it by touching the blade tips with a flag smeared with coloured chalk.
details.howItWorks: Each pitch link is a short rod with a ball joint at each end, running from the spinning upper swashplate to the pitch horn on one blade grip. As the swashplate tilts, the link for each blade rises and falls once every turn, twisting that blade's pitch up and down. Its length is adjustable with a threaded barrel so engineers can make all three blades fly in exactly the same plane.
keyNumbers: Three links, one per blade
Each moves up and down about 400 times a minute
Length adjusted in small fractions of a turn
details.madeOf: Steel or titanium tube with spherical rod-end bearings screwed into each end and locked. The parts must stay stiff and free of play, because any slack shows up as vibration in the cabin.

parts.name: Pitch link

parts.description: Two plates on a ball joint around the mast: the bottom one is tilted by the controls, the top one spins and passes the tilt to the blades.

details.didYouKnow: Because a spinning rotor reacts about a quarter-turn after a pitch change, the controls are rigged so each blade gets its extra pitch roughly 90 degrees before the point where the disc should tilt.
details.howItWorks: The swashplate turns the pilot's movements in the fixed cabin into blade movements on the spinning rotor. Raising the whole plate along the mast increases all blade pitches together for collective, while tilting it makes each blade's pitch rise and fall once per turn for cyclic. A scissor-shaped link drives the upper plate round with the mast, and a big bearing between the plates lets one spin while the other stays still.
keyNumbers: Upper plate spins at about 400 rpm
Usually moved by three hydraulic servos
Tilts only a few degrees in normal flight
details.madeOf: Machined steel or aluminium alloy rings with a large precision ball or roller bearing between them. It sits on a spherical ball so it can tilt in any direction.

parts.name: Swashplate

parts.description: Hollow steel shaft that carries the rotor's lift down into the airframe and its drive up from the gearbox.

details.didYouKnow: The big nut holding the rotor to the top of the mast is often nicknamed the Jesus nut, because if it ever came off there would be nothing left to do but pray.
details.howItWorks: The mast is the rotating shaft that the rotor hub sits on. It carries the engine's twisting drive up from the main gearbox, and at the same time the whole weight of the helicopter hangs from it in flight. The swashplate slides and tilts on a sleeve around its lower part, and a large retaining nut at the top holds the hub on.
keyNumbers: Turns at about 400 rpm
Carries a torque of roughly 14,000 newton-metres at full power
Supports up to about 22,000 newtons of lift
details.madeOf: A hollow forged steel shaft, machined and often shot-peened to resist fatigue cracking. Making it hollow saves weight while keeping almost all its stiffness.

parts.name: Rotor mast

parts.description: Streamlined cover over the engine and gearbox, opened for inspection before every flight.

details.didYouKnow: Many cowlings have built-in steps and handholds so the pilot can climb onto the roof to inspect the rotor head during the walk-around.
details.howItWorks: The cowling wraps the engine, gearbox and rotor controls on the cabin roof in a smooth shape that cuts drag and keeps out rain. Its panels hinge or lift off so the pilot can check oil levels, leaks and loose fittings before each flight. Inside, a fireproof firewall separates the hot engine bay from the gearbox and cabin.
keyNumbers: Panels typically weigh only a few kilograms each
Engine bay temperatures can exceed 100 degrees C nearby
Opened and checked before every flight day
details.madeOf: Light composite or thin aluminium panels, with fire-resistant material such as titanium or steel near the engine. Composites are easy to mould into curved, aerodynamic shapes.

parts.name: Engine cowling

parts.description: Reduces the engine's speed from tens of thousands of rpm to about 400 rpm at the rotor, and drives the tail shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Magnetic chip detectors in the oil collect tiny flakes of steel, and a warning light tells the pilot if metal is building up, often long before a gear actually fails.
details.howItWorks: The engine's output shaft enters the gearbox, where a pair of bevel gears turns the drive upwards and a planetary gear set slows it further and increases its turning force. The mast comes out of the top, and a second output drives the tail rotor shaft. A freewheel in the drive lets the rotor keep turning if the engine stops, which is what makes a safe gliding landing possible.
keyNumbers: Reduces about 6,000 rpm to about 400 rpm
Overall ratio roughly 15 to 1
Holds a few litres of its own oil
Handles about 600 kW
details.madeOf: Hardened steel gears and bearings in a cast aluminium or magnesium alloy case. The light alloy case saves weight, while the steel gears survive enormous tooth loads.

parts.name: Main gearbox

parts.description: Small gas turbine that burns kerosene and puts out about 600 kW through a spinning output shaft rather than a jet.

details.didYouKnow: For its weight a small turboshaft gives several times the power of a piston engine, which is why most helicopters bigger than a two-seater use one.
details.howItWorks: Air is squeezed by a compressor, mixed with kerosene and burned, and the hot gas spins turbines. One turbine drives the compressor to keep the engine running, and a separate free power turbine drives the output shaft to the gearbox, so the rotor can be held at a steady speed while the engine's core speeds up or slows down. An electronic or hydraulic governor adjusts fuel automatically to keep rotor rpm constant.
keyNumbers: About 600 kW, roughly 800 horsepower
Core spins at up to around 50,000 rpm
Weighs roughly 100 to 150 kg
Burns roughly 150 to 200 litres of fuel an hour
details.madeOf: Titanium and steel for the compressor, and nickel superalloys for the combustor and turbines, which glow in gas far hotter than steel could survive. Light alloys are used for casings that stay cool.

parts.name: Turboshaft engine

parts.description: Bent pipe that dumps the hot turbine exhaust up and away from the tail boom.

details.didYouKnow: Pilots watch the turbine temperature closely during start-up, because a slow or hung start can overheat the engine in seconds.
details.howItWorks: After the power turbine has taken most of the energy out of the hot gas, what is left leaves through the exhaust pipe. The pipe bends the flow upward and outward so the hot gas does not scorch the tail boom or blow into the air intake. Because the turbine extracts nearly all the useful energy, the exhaust gives almost no forward thrust.
keyNumbers: Exhaust gas typically around 500 degrees C
Gas leaves at fairly low speed compared with a jet
Usually a single outlet on a light helicopter
details.madeOf: Thin heat-resistant stainless steel or nickel alloy sheet, welded into shape. It must survive repeated heating and cooling without cracking.

parts.name: Engine exhaust

parts.description: Screened opening that feeds air to the engine and keeps out debris kicked up by the rotor.

details.didYouKnow: Damage from things sucked into an engine is called foreign object damage, and crews do walk-arounds partly to pick up loose objects near the helicopter before starting.
details.howItWorks: The intake guides air smoothly into the engine's compressor, which swallows a large volume every second. A screen or filter stops stones, grass, leaves and birds from getting in, since a single pebble can damage compressor blades spinning at tens of thousands of rpm. Some helicopters add particle separators or barrier filters for dusty or snowy work.
keyNumbers: Roughly 2 to 3 kg of air per second at full power
Mesh openings typically a few millimetres
Hot gas outlet kept well away from the inlet
details.madeOf: Moulded composite or plastic ducting with a stainless steel mesh screen. Composites can be shaped into smooth curves that keep the airflow even.

parts.name: Air intake

parts.description: Long shaft in sections, running along the top of the boom from the main gearbox to the tail gearbox.

details.didYouKnow: If the tail drive ever fails, the pilot cuts power and glides down in autorotation, because with no engine torque there is nothing for the tail rotor to fight.
details.howItWorks: The shaft carries power from the main gearbox all the way to the tail gearbox, so the tail rotor always turns in step with the main rotor. It is split into short sections joined by flexible couplings, because the tail boom bends slightly in flight and a single long shaft would whip or crack. Hanger bearings bolted along the boom hold each section straight.
keyNumbers: Spins at roughly 5,000 to 6,000 rpm
Runs about 5 to 6 m to the tail
Carries roughly 10 to 15 percent of engine power in a hover
details.madeOf: Thin-walled aluminium alloy or steel tubes with flexible steel or composite couplings. Thin tubes are light yet resist twisting very well.

parts.name: Tail rotor driveshaft

parts.description: Crash-resistant bag tank under the floor holding about 540 litres of jet fuel.

details.didYouKnow: In the United States, every newly built helicopter has had to have a crash-resistant fuel system since 2020, after accident studies showed post-crash fires were a major killer.
details.howItWorks: The tank sits low under the cabin floor near the helicopter's centre of gravity, so the balance changes little as fuel is burned. An electric boost pump feeds the engine, and a sender reports the level to the cockpit. The tank is a flexible bladder with self-sealing breakaway fittings, so in a crash it is more likely to deform than burst.
keyNumbers: About 540 litres of jet fuel
Weighs roughly 430 kg when full
Enough for roughly 3 hours of flying
details.madeOf: Tough, flexible rubberised fabric or moulded polymer, often reinforced with nylon or aramid fibres. Flexibility lets it absorb impact rather than split.

parts.name: Fuel tank

parts.description: Aluminium and composite shell around the cabin; the floor and roof beams carry the loads from the rotor and skids.

details.didYouKnow: Much of the shell is only about a millimetre or so thick; its strength comes from shape and stiffening frames rather than thick metal.
details.howItWorks: The shell is the helicopter's body: a frame of beams and bulkheads covered with a thin skin that together carry loads like an eggshell. The main gearbox bolts to the roof structure, so the rotor's lift travels down through it, while the skids bolt to the floor beams underneath. The floor is also designed to crush in a controlled way in a very hard landing to protect the people inside.
keyNumbers: Empty helicopter weighs roughly 1,200 to 1,300 kg
Cabin seats five
Fuselage about 1.9 m wide
details.madeOf: Riveted aluminium alloy frames and skins, with composite panels for curved shapes such as the roof and fairings. Aluminium is cheap, light and easy to repair; composites save weight where shapes are complex.

parts.name: Cabin shell

parts.description: Large curved windscreen giving the pilot a view forwards and down past their feet.

details.didYouKnow: Bird strikes are a real risk at low level, and some helicopters can be fitted with thicker, bird-resistant windscreens for that reason.
details.howItWorks: The large curved transparency forms the whole front of the cabin, giving the pilot a wide view ahead and, through lower chin windows, straight down past the pedals to the landing spot. Being able to see the ground directly below is vital when hovering, landing on slopes or working with a sling load. Its curve also helps it stay stiff and smooth to the airflow.
keyNumbers: Typically a few millimetres thick
Covers well over 180 degrees of view
Weighs a fraction of an equivalent glass screen
details.madeOf: Formed acrylic or polycarbonate plastic rather than real glass, shaped by heating sheets over a mould. Plastic is much lighter than glass and can be made into compound curves.

parts.name: Nose canopy

parts.description: Hinged door with a large window; it can be removed for filming or hoist work.

details.didYouKnow: When a helicopter flies with doors off, loose items in the cabin must be secured, because anything that blows out can strike the tail rotor.
details.howItWorks: The left front door opens beside the front passenger or co-pilot seat, swinging forwards on hinges at its front edge. The large window gives that occupant a clear view down and to the side, which suits an observer or camera operator. Because the left seat is not the pilot's, this is the door most often taken off for aerial filming or photography.
keyNumbers: Typically weighs only several kilograms
Removed in minutes by pulling the hinge pins
Reduced airspeed limit when flown off
details.madeOf: A light frame of aluminium or composite holding a large clear acrylic or polycarbonate window. Keeping it light makes it easy for one person to lift off its hinges.

parts.name: Cabin door (left)

parts.description: Hinged door with a large window; it can be removed for filming or hoist work.

details.didYouKnow: Pilots traditionally board from the right and walk round the front of the helicopter, keeping well away from the spinning tail rotor at the back.
details.howItWorks: The right front door is the pilot's door, beside the seat where the pilot sits with the cyclic in the right hand. It has a vent or sliding window on many types so the pilot can get fresh air or talk to ground crew. Opening it in flight is restricted, because the airflow can pull it wide and push against its hinges.
keyNumbers: Typically weighs only several kilograms
Pilot usually boards on this side
Can be removed for hoist or utility work
details.madeOf: Aluminium or composite frame with a curved clear plastic window and a simple latch. Light materials keep the door easy to remove and refit.

parts.name: Cabin door (right)

parts.description: Tapering tube that holds the tail rotor far enough back to counter the main rotor's torque.

details.didYouKnow: In a hover the tail rotor can use roughly 10 to 15 percent of the engine's power just to stop the helicopter turning.
details.howItWorks: The rotor's twisting force tries to spin the fuselage, and the tail rotor fights it with a sideways push. The longer the boom, the more leverage that push has, so the tail rotor can be smaller and use less power. The boom also carries the tail driveshaft along its top and the fin, stabiliser and tail gearbox at its end.
keyNumbers: Tail rotor roughly 6 m behind the mast
Tail rotor thrust roughly 200 to 300 kg force at full power
Boom tapers to well under half its root width
details.madeOf: A riveted aluminium tube made of thin skins and ring frames, tapering towards the tail. This light tube resists bending and twisting very efficiently.

parts.name: Tail boom

parts.description: Fin that keeps the helicopter pointing into the airflow in forward flight, easing the tail rotor's job.

details.didYouKnow: Because the fin unloads the tail rotor in cruise, pilots need less pedal at speed than in a hover, where the tail rotor does all the work alone.
details.howItWorks: Like the feathers on an arrow, the fin keeps the tail trailing behind and the nose pointing into the wind in forward flight. It is often shaped like a sideways wing so that at cruising speed it makes a sideways force that does much of the tail rotor's anti-torque job. That lets the tail rotor run at lower pitch, saving power. A lower part of the fin often carries a skid to protect the tail rotor if the tail touches the ground.
keyNumbers: Typically around 1 m tall
Most useful above roughly 100 km/h
Weighs only a few kilograms
details.madeOf: Aluminium or composite skins over light ribs and spars. Composites suit the curved aerofoil shape and resist corrosion.

parts.name: Vertical fin

parts.description: Small tailplane that keeps the fuselage level in forward flight.

details.didYouKnow: A stabiliser is often shaped like an upside-down wing, because its job is to push the tail down rather than lift it up.
details.howItWorks: When the pilot tilts the rotor forward to speed up, the fuselage tends to hang nose-down beneath it. The stabiliser, a small wing at the back, pushes the tail down in forward flight to bring the fuselage back towards level, cutting drag and improving the pilot's view. Unlike an aeroplane's tailplane, it is usually fixed and not moved by the pilot.
keyNumbers: Typically about 2 m across
Mounted roughly 5 to 6 m behind the mast
Weighs only a few kilograms
details.madeOf: Aluminium or composite skins over a light structure, sometimes with small fins on its tips. Light materials matter because weight at the very end of the boom shifts the balance a lot.

parts.name: Horizontal stabiliser

parts.description: Right-angle gearbox that turns the driveshaft's spin through 90 degrees to drive the tail rotor.

details.didYouKnow: Pilots check a small sight glass on the tail gearbox during the walk-around to make sure its oil level is correct.
details.howItWorks: The tail driveshaft arrives horizontally along the boom, and a pair of bevel gears inside turns the drive sideways to spin the tail rotor. The gearbox also sets the tail rotor's speed relative to the main rotor, so the two always turn in a fixed ratio. The pitch-change rod from the pedals usually passes through its hollow output shaft to reach the tail hub.
keyNumbers: Turns the drive through 90 degrees
Output about 2,600 rpm
Holds well under a litre of its own oil
details.madeOf: Hardened steel spiral bevel gears and bearings in a cast aluminium or magnesium alloy case. Spiral teeth mesh smoothly and quietly under heavy load.

parts.name: Tail rotor gearbox

parts.description: Hub that holds the two tail blades and changes their pitch when the pilot presses the pedals.

details.didYouKnow: The tail hub is often set at a skewed hinge angle so that when a blade flaps, its pitch automatically reduces a little, which helps keep the blades from flapping too far.
details.howItWorks: The hub holds both tail blades and lets them rock together like a seesaw, so as one flaps one way the other flaps the opposite way, evening out the uneven airflow across the tail. A sliding sleeve and links twist both blades at once when the pilot moves the pedals, increasing or reducing the sideways thrust. Because the tail rotor spins so fast, small pitch changes make a big difference in thrust.
keyNumbers: Spins at about 2,600 rpm
Carries two blades 180 degrees apart
Pitch range of roughly 30 degrees or so
details.madeOf: Machined steel or titanium, with sealed bearings or elastomeric pads for the pitch-change motion. It must be strong yet compact and light at the far end of the boom.

parts.name: Tail rotor hub

parts.description: Short blade spinning about 2,600 rpm; its sideways thrust stops the fuselage spinning.

details.didYouKnow: Many tail rotors are set to turn with the blade at the top moving backwards, because tests found that direction works better with the main rotor's wake.
details.howItWorks: This blade is a small, fast wing that pushes air sideways to stop the fuselage turning against the main rotor. At the top of its circle it passes closest to the main rotor's downwash, and that changing airflow is one reason the two tail blades are linked on a seesaw hub to share out the loads. The upper and lower blades are identical, and each one passes the top of the circle about 40 times a second.
keyNumbers: Rotor roughly 1.9 m across
About 2,600 rpm
Tips moving at over 200 m/s
details.madeOf: Composite skins of glass or carbon fibre around a foam core, with a metal leading-edge strip against erosion. Composites keep the blade light and stiff at very high speeds.

parts.name: Tail rotor blade (upper)

parts.description: Short blade spinning about 2,600 rpm; its sideways thrust stops the fuselage spinning.

details.didYouKnow: A running tail rotor is nearly invisible, which is why ground crews are trained never to walk towards the tail of a helicopter with the rotors turning.
details.howItWorks: This blade makes exactly the same sideways thrust as its partner, but at the bottom of its arc it passes closest to the ground, people and long grass. The fin's lower tail skid helps keep it clear if the tail drops during a landing or flare. Because the two blades are joined on one hub, any damage to one quickly shows up as heavy vibration.
keyNumbers: About 2,600 rpm
Roughly 0.8 m long
Spinning so fast it is almost invisible
details.madeOf: Glass or carbon fibre composite over a foam core with a metal erosion strip. The material is light enough to keep the spinning loads down at very high rpm.

parts.name: Tail rotor blade (lower)

parts.description: Aluminium tube the helicopter rests on; its upturned front lets it slide on landing.

details.didYouKnow: If one skid stays stuck to the ground, or catches on something, while the helicopter rolls towards it, it can tip over on that skid; pilots call this dynamic rollover.
details.howItWorks: The left skid is one of two long rails the helicopter stands on, bolted to the ends of the front and rear cross tubes. Its upturned front lets it slide rather than dig in if the helicopter touches down while still moving forward. Replaceable wear plates on its underside take the scraping instead of the tube itself.
keyNumbers: Typically around 2.5 m long
Skids roughly 2 to 2.5 m apart
Tube roughly 7 to 10 cm across
details.madeOf: Seamless aluminium alloy tube with steel wear shoes riveted underneath. Aluminium keeps the gear light; the shoes save the tube from abrasion on concrete.

parts.name: Skid tube (left)

parts.description: Aluminium tube the helicopter rests on; its upturned front lets it slide on landing.

details.didYouKnow: Inflatable emergency floats can be packed along each skid and blown up in seconds from a gas bottle if the helicopter has to land on water.
details.howItWorks: The right skid mirrors the left and is on the pilot's side, where a step on the cross tube or skid helps the pilot climb aboard. Brackets on the skids are used to clip on ground-handling wheels, so the helicopter can be pushed into a hangar. They are also the mounting points for options such as emergency floats or bear-paw plates for snow.
keyNumbers: Typically around 2.5 m long
Gear weighs roughly 50 to 70 kg in total
Ground wheels lift it a few centimetres
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy tube with replaceable steel wear shoes. The gear is made light because every kilogram saved can be carried as fuel or payload.

parts.name: Skid tube (right)

parts.description: Bowed tube joining the skids to the airframe; it flexes to soak up a hard landing.

details.didYouKnow: After a hard landing, engineers measure how far apart the skids have spread; if the cross tubes have bent past a limit, they are replaced.
details.howItWorks: The front cross tube runs under the forward cabin and joins the two skids to the airframe. Its bow acts like a spring: in a normal landing it flexes and returns, and in a very hard one it bends permanently to soak up energy before the cabin is hit. Its stiffness is also tuned to help keep the gear from shaking in step with the rotor on the ground.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 2 to 2.5 m
Flexes a few centimetres in a firm landing
Checked for permanent spread after hard landings
details.madeOf: Heat-treated aluminium alloy tube, bent to shape. The alloy is chosen to flex elastically for normal landings yet bend, rather than snap, in an extreme one.

parts.name: Cross tube (front)

parts.description: Bowed tube joining the skids to the airframe; it flexes to soak up a hard landing.

details.didYouKnow: Skid gear has no oil, tyres or hydraulics, which is why light helicopters use it: it is cheap, light and needs very little maintenance.
details.howItWorks: The rear cross tube sits under the back of the cabin and does the same springy job as the front tube. With the front tube it forms a four-point mount that carries the helicopter's weight into the floor beams. Setting the two tubes well apart, either side of the rotor mast, gives the helicopter a stable stance on the ground.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 2 to 2.5 m
Shares the load of up to about 2,250 kg
Bolted to the airframe at two points
details.madeOf: Bent, heat-treated aluminium alloy tube, often with a step or fairing attached. Aluminium gives a good balance of springiness and lightness.

parts.name: Cross tube (rear)

parts.description: Glass display and gauges showing rotor and engine speed, airspeed, altitude and attitude.

details.didYouKnow: Many helicopter displays combine several engine limits into one needle or number, so the pilot sees at a glance how close they are to the most limiting one.
details.howItWorks: The panel gathers the readings the pilot needs most: rotor speed, engine torque and turbine temperature on one side, and airspeed, altitude and attitude on the other. Rotor speed is critical, because if it drops too low the blades cannot make enough lift, so a horn and light warn the pilot. The panel is kept low and small so the pilot can see out through the nose canopy.
keyNumbers: Rotor speed kept near 100 percent of normal
Low rotor rpm horn sounds a few percent below that
Typically one or two glass display screens
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic or composite shroud on an aluminium frame, holding electronic displays and backup mechanical gauges. The shroud cuts glare on the screens.

parts.name: Instrument panel

parts.description: Front seat beside the pilot, often with removable dual controls.

details.didYouKnow: Flight instructors usually sit in the left seat, so trainees learn from the start in the right-hand pilot's position they will use later.
details.howItWorks: The left front seat sits beside the pilot and is usually taken by a passenger, an observer or an instructor. With dual controls fitted, a second cyclic, collective and pedals let someone fly from this seat too; for passengers, those controls are often removed so they cannot be bumped. Like the pilot's seat it is built to stroke downwards in a crash to absorb energy.
keyNumbers: Four or five point harness
Designed for crash loads of roughly 30 g
Dual controls removable in minutes
details.madeOf: A light metal or composite frame with fabric covering and foam cushions. The structure is designed to crumple in a controlled way rather than stay rigid.

parts.name: Front passenger seat (left)

parts.description: Energy-absorbing seat for the pilot, who sits on the right in most helicopters.

details.didYouKnow: One common explanation for the right-hand seat is that the pilot can keep the right hand on the cyclic and use the left to work radios and switches in the centre console.
details.howItWorks: The pilot sits on the right with the cyclic in the right hand and the collective in the left. The seat is fixed in a set position so the pilot's arms and legs reach the controls naturally, and its frame is built to crush downward in a crash, absorbing energy that would otherwise reach the spine. A shoulder harness holds the pilot firmly in place.
keyNumbers: Four or five point harness
Designed for crash loads of roughly 30 g
Pilot's right hand stays on the cyclic
details.madeOf: Aluminium or composite frame with energy-absorbing parts, covered in fabric over foam. The materials balance comfort on long flights with crash protection.

parts.name: Pilot seat (right)

parts.description: Bench for three passengers across the back of the cabin.

details.didYouKnow: Before every flight the pilot works out the total weight and balance, because a helicopter loaded too far forward or back may run out of cyclic control.
details.howItWorks: The bench seats three passengers side by side across the back of the cabin. It sits roughly beneath the rotor, so adding or removing passengers shifts the helicopter's balance much less than loading people in the nose. The cushions can often be folded or removed to turn the space into a cargo area or make room for a stretcher.
keyNumbers: Seats three passengers
Each with its own lap or shoulder belt
Bench weighs roughly 15 to 25 kg
details.madeOf: A light aluminium or composite frame with foam cushions and hard-wearing fabric or leather covers. Quick-release fittings let it come out without tools.

parts.name: Rear bench seat

parts.description: Stick between the pilot's knees that tilts the rotor disc to move forwards, backwards or sideways.

details.didYouKnow: In a hover the cyclic is so sensitive that new pilots often overcontrol; experienced pilots describe flying it with pressure rather than visible movement.
details.howItWorks: Moving the cyclic tilts the swashplate, which makes each blade's pitch rise and fall once per turn, or cyclically, which gives the stick its name. That tilts the rotor disc in the direction the stick is pushed, and the helicopter follows. Hydraulic servos do most of the work, so the stick needs only light, precise movements, and buttons on its grip handle the radio and trim.
keyNumbers: Blade pitch changed about 6 to 7 times a second
Moves the rotor disc a few degrees
Usually hydraulically boosted
details.madeOf: A steel or aluminium stick with a moulded plastic or rubber grip. The grip holds switches the pilot can reach without letting go.

parts.name: Cyclic stick

parts.description: Lever beside the pilot's seat that raises or lowers the pitch of all main blades together, with the throttle twist-grip on its end.

details.didYouKnow: If the engine stops, the pilot lowers the collective at once, so the air flowing up through the rotor keeps it spinning like a windmill for a controlled glide down.
details.howItWorks: Raising the collective lifts the whole swashplate, increasing the pitch of all three blades at once so the rotor makes more lift and the helicopter climbs. More pitch means more drag on the blades, so the engine governor adds fuel to keep rotor rpm steady. A friction knob lets the pilot set how stiff it feels, and the twist-grip throttle is mostly used at start-up and shutdown.
keyNumbers: Blade pitch range roughly 0 to 15 degrees
Lowered fully in an autorotation
Pivots beside the pilot's left hip
details.madeOf: Steel or aluminium tube with a plastic grip and switch box at its end. It is strong enough to be leaned on in turbulence.

parts.name: Collective lever

parts.description: Foot pedals that change the tail rotor's pitch to point the nose left or right.

details.didYouKnow: Unlike an aeroplane's rudder pedals, a helicopter's pedals are used constantly in a hover, and the pilot needs more pedal on one side than the other just to hold a heading.
details.howItWorks: Pushing one pedal increases the tail rotor's pitch and thrust, and the other reduces it, swinging the nose left or right. In a hover, every change in collective changes the main rotor's torque, so the pilot must add or remove pedal at the same time to stop the nose wandering. The pedals connect to the tail hub through rods or cables running the length of the boom.
keyNumbers: Pedal travel typically several centimetres each way
Controls roughly 200 to 300 kg force of tail thrust
Linkage runs roughly 6 m to the tail
details.madeOf: Steel or aluminium pedals and linkage with adjustable positions for different leg lengths. Steel parts take the force of a pilot pushing hard.

parts.name: Anti-torque pedals

summary: A five-seat light helicopter: one turboshaft engine drives a three-blade main rotor about 10.7 m across and a small tail rotor, letting it take off vertically, hover and fly at around 230 km/h.

name: Diesel-Electric Submarine
overview:
A submarine is a ship that can sink on purpose and come back up. It does this with ballast tanks between its two hulls: opening vents lets seawater flood in so it gets heavier and dives, and blowing compressed air into the tanks pushes the water out so it rises. Once submerged, small trims of water and the angle of its planes keep it hovering at any depth, like a fish.

The crew live and work inside the pressure hull, a thick steel cylinder that keeps out the crushing weight of the sea; every 10 m of depth adds another atmosphere of pressure. Around it, the outer casing gives a smooth, quiet shape and is covered in rubbery tiles that soak up sonar pings.

This boat is diesel-electric. On or near the surface it runs diesel generators, breathing through a snorkel mast, to charge huge banks of batteries. Deep underwater it shuts the diesels off and runs on battery power alone: an electric motor turns a large, slow propeller, which makes it one of the quietest machines in the ocean. It hunts by listening with sonar arrays in the bow and attacks with torpedoes fired from tubes at the front.

parts.description: Streamlined free-flooding nose that houses the sonar array and the muzzles of the torpedo tubes.

details.didYouKnow: Early submarines had sharp, ship-like bows for running on the surface; once boats spent most of their time submerged, designers switched to the rounded whale-like nose because it is quieter and faster underwater.
details.howItWorks: The bow is not watertight: it fills with sea as the boat dives, so it never has to resist depth pressure, only give the boat a smooth rounded nose. Behind its skin sit the bow sonar, the forward main ballast tank and the front ends of the six torpedo tubes, whose muzzles open through small shutter doors that close flush to keep the flow quiet. Its blunt, rounded shape suits a boat that spends most of its life underwater rather than ploughing through waves.
keyNumbers: Roughly 6 to 8 m long
Six torpedo muzzles about 0.5 m across
Floods fully within seconds of diving
details.madeOf: Mild or high-strength steel plating for the structure, with panels of glass-reinforced plastic in front of the sonar. GRP lets sound pass through almost unchanged while staying tough and corrosion-free.

parts.name: Bow section

parts.description: Light outer skin over the middle of the boat, covered in rubbery anechoic tiles that absorb sonar.

details.didYouKnow: Anechoic tiles can occasionally come loose at sea, and photos of boats returning to port sometimes show gaps like missing teeth where tiles have been lost.
details.howItWorks: The casing is a thin fairing wrapped around the top and sides of the pressure hull, giving a flat deck to walk on when surfaced and a smooth shape underwater. The gap between it and the pressure hull is free-flooding and holds pipes, mooring gear, the flank sonar arrays and the compressed-air bottles outside the crew's living space. Its anechoic tiles soak up incoming sonar pings and also damp the hum of machinery leaking out from inside.
keyNumbers: Tiles typically a few cm thick
Thousands of tiles cover the boat
Plating only a few mm to about 1 cm thick
details.madeOf: Fairly thin steel plate or glass-reinforced plastic panels, with tiles of specially formulated rubber or polyurethane glued on. The tiles contain tiny voids that turn sound energy into a little heat.

parts.name: Outer casing half

parts.description: Tapering tail cone that smooths the flow of water into the propeller.

details.didYouKnow: The teardrop hull with a single propeller at a pointed tail came out of research in the 1950s and is still the basic shape of most submarines, because it is so efficient and quiet underwater.
details.howItWorks: The stern cone narrows the hull smoothly so water flowing along the sides closes in gently on the propeller instead of tumbling off a blunt edge. Getting this flow even all the way round matters, because uneven flow makes each blade feel a pulsing load, which shows up as noise on enemy sonar. The X-form planes are mounted on the cone, and the propeller shaft runs out through its tip to the hub.
keyNumbers: Roughly 10 m of taper
Narrows from about 6.6 m to under 1 m
Overall hull about 10 times as long as it is wide
details.madeOf: Steel plating shaped over internal frames, faired and coated like the rest of the casing. Much of it is free-flooding, so it only needs to be stiff, not pressure-proof.

parts.name: Stern section

parts.description: Tall fin on top that holds the masts and periscopes and gives the bridge a lookout spot when surfaced.

details.didYouKnow: Some navies call this the sail and others the fin; both names replaced the older term conning tower, which on early boats was a real watertight room.
details.howItWorks: The sail is a streamlined fin that sheathes the masts and periscopes when they are lowered, so they slide up and down inside it without sticking out into the flow. When surfaced, the crew climb up a trunk to a small open bridge at the top, which is the only high lookout point on a boat that otherwise sits barely above the waves. It sits above the control room so the optical periscope can pass straight down into it.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 to 5 m tall above the casing
About 8 to 10 m long
Holds four or so retractable masts
details.madeOf: Steel or glass-reinforced plastic plating over a steel frame, free-flooding inside. The sail is not part of the pressure hull, so it can be built light.

parts.name: Sail (fin)

parts.description: Small wings on the sail that steer the boat up or down near the surface and at periscope depth.

details.didYouKnow: Some deep-ocean submarines can turn their sail planes vertical so the sail can push up through sea ice without snapping them off.
details.howItWorks: Each plane is a small hydrofoil that the crew tilt from the control room; angling it makes water push the front of the boat up or down. Mounting them high on the sail keeps them away from the bow sonar, so the swirling water they create does not drown out what the sonar is listening to. They are especially useful at periscope depth, where the boat must hold its height within a metre or so while waves try to push it around.
keyNumbers: Each roughly 2 to 3 m span
Swing typically up to about 25 degrees
Depth held within about 1 m at periscope depth
details.madeOf: High-strength steel spars covered in shaped plating, turned by hydraulic actuators inside the sail. They need to be stiff enough not to flutter at speed.

parts.name: Sail planes

parts.description: One of four rudder-planes set in an X; together they steer and control depth, and still work if one jams.

details.didYouKnow: X-form sterns were first tried on an experimental teardrop-hulled submarine in the 1960s, but they only caught on widely once computers could blend the four fin movements automatically.
details.howItWorks: Instead of a cross of separate rudders and hydroplanes, four identical fins stick out diagonally from the tail. A computer moves all four together in different combinations, so that the same fins steer left and right and pitch the boat up and down. Because every fin contributes to both jobs, a single jammed fin can be balanced by the other three, and the diagonal layout keeps the fins within the hull's width for berthing and sitting on the seabed.
keyNumbers: 4 independent fins
Each roughly 2 to 3 m long
Set at about 45 degrees to the vertical
details.madeOf: High-strength steel structure with smooth plating, each fin driven by its own hydraulic actuator. Separate actuators are what give the redundancy.

parts.name: X-form stern plane

parts.description: Retractable planes near the bow that tilt the nose up or down; they fold away when surfaced.

details.didYouKnow: Planes work like an aircraft's wings but underwater, and because water is about 800 times denser than air, a fin the size of a door can push hard enough to steer a boat of nearly 2,000 tonnes.
details.howItWorks: These small hydrofoils sit low on the bow and act on the front of the boat, the opposite end from the stern planes. Tilting them changes the boat's angle and depth together, giving fine control at slow speed when the stern planes have little bite. When the boat surfaces or comes alongside, they rotate and fold flat against the hull so waves and harbour walls cannot damage them.
keyNumbers: Each roughly 2 m span
Fold away in well under a minute
Most effective at a few knots
details.madeOf: Steel spars and plating on a pivoting shaft that passes into the hull through a watertight seal, worked by hydraulics. Folding gear adds weight, so the planes are kept compact.

parts.name: Bow diving planes

parts.description: Thick high-strength steel cylinder that keeps the sea out; the crew and machinery live inside it.

details.didYouKnow: Designers usually build in a margin so the hull would only collapse at roughly one and a half times its test depth, the deepest the boat routinely goes.
details.howItWorks: The pressure hull is a long cylinder stiffened by steel ring frames every metre or so, which stop the shell from buckling inwards. At depth, the sea squeezes it evenly from all sides and the hull actually shrinks slightly, which the crew can hear as creaks. Everything that must stay dry and at normal air pressure lives inside, and every hole through it, from hatches to pipes, is a carefully designed weak point.
keyNumbers: About 6 m in diameter
Steel typically a few cm thick
Test depth typically a few hundred metres
About 30 atmospheres of sea pressure at 300 m
details.madeOf: Special high-yield steel, made tough enough to bend slightly rather than crack, and welded under strict control. Each weld is X-rayed or ultrasonically checked, because one flaw could start a failure.

parts.name: Pressure hull half

parts.description: Domed end cap closing the pressure hull; domes spread the sea's push evenly, like an egg.

details.didYouKnow: For the same thickness, a hemisphere is about twice as strong as a cylinder against outside pressure, which is why the ends of pressure vessels are domed rather than flat.
details.howItWorks: The forward dome closes off the front of the pressure hull and sees the full sea pressure head-on. A dome carries load as pure compression spread evenly in every direction, which is far more efficient than a flat wall. This one is also pierced by the rear ends of the six torpedo tubes, so their breech doors open into the torpedo room just inside it, and each penetration is heavily reinforced.
keyNumbers: About 6 m across
6 torpedo tube penetrations
Bulges forward about 1 to 2 m
details.madeOf: The same high-yield steel as the hull, pressed or spun into a curved shape and welded to the cylinder. Thicker rings are added around each torpedo tube opening.

parts.name: Pressure hull end dome (forward)

parts.description: Tank between the hulls that floods with seawater to dive and is blown out with compressed air to surface.

details.didYouKnow: Main ballast tanks are either fully flooded or fully empty in normal use; the fine balancing at depth is done with much smaller trim tanks inside the pressure hull.
details.howItWorks: The forward tank wraps around the front of the pressure hull with open flood holes at the bottom and vent valves at the top. Opening the vents lets air escape so the sea rushes in from below and the boat loses its spare buoyancy; to surface, the vents shut and compressed air is blown in, pushing the water back out through the holes. Being at the bow, it also controls whether the nose goes down first when diving.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 100 tonnes of water
Vents open to dive in about a minute
Front edge about 20 m forward of the boat's centre
details.madeOf: Steel plating that only has to withstand small pressure differences, because the tank is open to the sea at the bottom. It is coated heavily against corrosion since it is often wet.

parts.name: Main ballast tank (forward)

parts.description: Domed end cap closing the pressure hull; domes spread the sea's push evenly, like an egg.

details.didYouKnow: Stern glands are designed to let a tiny trickle of seawater through to lubricate and cool the seal; it is pumped away from a small drain well inside the boat.
details.howItWorks: The aft dome seals the back of the pressure hull just behind the propulsion motor. Its key feature is the opening for the propeller shaft, which turns continuously through a stern gland that has to stop seawater getting in while letting the shaft spin and slide slightly as the hull squeezes. The thrust of the propeller is fed into the hull structure just inside it through a thrust bearing.
keyNumbers: About 6 m across
1 shaft penetration about 0.3 m wide
Faces the same sea pressure as the forward dome
details.madeOf: High-yield steel matching the hull, with a thick machined boss around the shaft opening to carry the gland and spread the loads.

parts.name: Pressure hull end dome (aft)

parts.description: Tank between the hulls that floods with seawater to dive and is blown out with compressed air to surface.

details.didYouKnow: A single-hull boat like this one has much less spare buoyancy on the surface than a double-hulled design, so it floats low, with waves often washing over the casing.
details.howItWorks: The aft tank does the same job as the forward one at the other end of the boat, so together they lift or sink the hull evenly. Divers can flood the two tanks a moment apart to put a gentle bow-down angle on as the boat leaves the surface. When surfacing in a hurry, both are blown hard together so the boat rises level rather than shooting up nose-first.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 100 tonnes of water
Together the tanks give about 10 to 15 percent spare buoyancy
Sits about 20 m aft of centre
details.madeOf: Steel plating with flood openings at the bottom and vent valves at the top, shaped to follow the narrowing stern. Like the forward tank it needs good paint to resist constant wetting.

parts.name: Main ballast tank (aft)

parts.description: Steel wall dividing the pressure hull into compartments, so one flooded section doesn't sink the boat.

details.didYouKnow: Many small diesel-electric boats have only two or three compartments, so each bulkhead protects a large share of the crew; escape hatches are usually placed so each end of the boat has one.
details.howItWorks: This aft bulkhead separates the living and battery spaces from the engine room, where the diesels and the propulsion motor run. It keeps engine noise, heat and any fire or flooding in the machinery space from spreading forward. A watertight door lets crew pass through, and it is shut whenever the boat goes to action stations or something goes wrong.
keyNumbers: About 6 m across
Door typically roughly 0.7 to 0.8 m wide
Dozens of sealed cable and pipe glands
details.madeOf: Welded steel plate, often slightly dished or heavily stiffened, with a circular door and many sealed fittings for cables and pipes passing through.

parts.name: Watertight bulkhead 1

parts.description: Steel wall dividing the pressure hull into compartments, so one flooded section doesn't sink the boat.

details.didYouKnow: Watertight doors on submarines are usually round or oval because curves have no corners where stress concentrates, so they can be lighter for the same strength.
details.howItWorks: This forward bulkhead sits roughly beneath the sail, dividing the torpedo room and control area from the accommodation behind. If the bow section flooded, for example from a damaged torpedo tube, closing its door would keep the rest of the boat dry. It also gives a firm anchor for the weapon handling gear and forward equipment.
keyNumbers: About 6 m across
Roughly 7 m forward of the boat's centre
Door typically roughly 0.7 to 0.8 m wide
details.madeOf: Welded steel plate stiffened with ribs, with a circular watertight door and sealed penetrations. Being near the heavy torpedo stowage, it is built stoutly.

parts.name: Watertight bulkhead 2

parts.description: Banks of high-pressure air used to blow the ballast tanks and surface in an emergency.

details.didYouKnow: As compressed air rushes out of the bottles it cools sharply, which is why valves in blow systems can ice up and why designers fit filters and keep the air very dry.
details.howItWorks: Compressors on board squeeze ordinary air into these steel bottles, which are stored outside the pressure hull. When the boat needs to surface, valves release this air into the main ballast tanks, where it expands and pushes the seawater out. In an emergency blow, the crew release a large amount at once so the boat rises fast even if it is heavy with flooding.
keyNumbers: Stored at roughly 200 to 300 bar
Several thousand litres of bottle volume in total
An emergency blow can empty the tanks in about a minute
details.madeOf: Thick seamless steel cylinders, forged or drawn from solid billets so there are no welds to fail at very high pressure.

parts.name: Compressed-air bottles

parts.description: Cylinder of hundreds of underwater microphones that listens for ships and submarines miles away.

details.didYouKnow: Sound travels about 1,500 m per second in seawater, more than four times faster than in air, and it bends with temperature layers, so sonar operators study the water itself as much as the targets.
details.howItWorks: Rows of hydrophones arranged around a cylinder each pick up sound slightly earlier or later depending on its direction. Computers combine these tiny delays to form listening beams pointing in many directions at once, building a picture of noises all around the bow. It mostly listens passively, since sending a ping would give the boat away, but it can transmit if needed.
keyNumbers: Typically several hundred hydrophones
About 2 to 3 m across
Can detect noisy ships tens of km away
details.madeOf: Piezoelectric ceramic elements, which make a voltage when squeezed by sound, set in rubber or plastic mountings and housed behind an acoustically transparent window.

parts.name: Bow sonar array

parts.description: Steel tube with a watertight door at each end; water or air pressure pushes the torpedo out.

details.didYouKnow: The 533 mm tube size dates back more than a century and is still used by many navies today, so torpedoes are almost always built to fit it.
details.howItWorks: A torpedo is loaded from inside through the rear door, then the tube is flooded and pressure-equalised with the sea before the bow cap opens. A burst of water or air pushes the weapon out, or in some designs the torpedo simply swims out under its own power. An interlock stops both doors ever being open at once, because that would flood the torpedo room.
keyNumbers: 533 mm (21 inch) bore
About 7 m long
6 tubes, all in the bow
Reloading takes typically several minutes per tube
details.madeOf: Thick steel tube machined smooth inside, with heavy hinged doors at each end and an internal guide rail. The tube is part of the pressure boundary, so it is built to hull standards.

parts.name: Torpedo tube

parts.description: Wire-guided torpedo about 6 m long that steers itself to the target with its own sonar.

details.didYouKnow: Modern heavyweight torpedoes are designed to explode beneath a ship rather than hit it, so the bubble from the blast lifts and then drops the hull, breaking its back.
details.howItWorks: Once launched, the torpedo pays out a thin wire from spools on both itself and the boat, so the submarine can steer it using its own better sonar. As it closes in, the torpedo's sonar in its nose takes over, either listening or pinging to home in. An electric motor or a heat engine spins its contra-rotating propellers or pump-jet.
keyNumbers: About 6 m long
Roughly 1.5 tonnes
Up to about 50 knots
Range typically tens of km
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel body sections, with the warhead at the front, electronics and batteries or fuel in the middle, and the motor at the back.

parts.name: Heavyweight torpedo
